data.title: Network Rail blames dried-up soil for slowing down trains
data.description:
Network Rail has blamed dried-out soil for slowing down Britain’s trains.

Services in parts of East Anglia and the South West will have their speed restricted from next month, Network Rail has said, as drought shrinks the soil around tracks and makes it unsafe to operate at full speed.

Great Northern trains on the “Fen Line” between Ely in Cambridgeshire and King’s Lynn in Norfolk will be subject to speed restrictions from Monday Aug 3, with some services withdrawn and remaining ones taking longer. Trains may also run with fewer carriages.

Disruption could extend to other areas if rain does not fall soon.

Similar problems are expected to be confirmed this week on the west of England line between Salisbury and Exeter, with top speeds to be cut from the usual 85mph to 40mph.

Network Rail said: “Following England’s warmest spring on record and hot summer so far, the peat and clay that sits under long stretches of the railway on Anglia has dried out and shrunk. This has caused the track to drop in places and become uneven.

“These speed restrictions will need to be in place until the ground conditions have recovered, which can take some time.”

Britain’s railways have become increasingly beset by weather-related difficulties, including landslides following heavy rain, which killed two people near Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, in 2020 and derailed an express at Shap, Cumbria, last year. Damage from waves after heavy storms is also a problem, with the Great Western line through Devon especially vulnerable.

Warmer summers have also led to faster tree-growth, with increased instances of branches striking trains, forcing Network Rail to reassess its timetable for keeping vegetation in check.

As well as causing trains to run more slowly, the soil issues mean the “Fen Line” will need specialist maintenance later this month and again in September to stop the track deteriorating further.

Passengers will be forced to use buses while the work is completed. Greater Anglia, c2c and Elizabeth Line routes in Essex will also require work, according to Network Rail.

Heatwave impact

The slowdown follows extensive disruption to the railway earlier this summer, when the heatwave caused rails to buckle and set off lineside fires that forced key routes, including the West Coast Main Line (WCML), to close.

While the problem of shrinking soil was relatively new, it led to the imposition of emergency timetables in 2022 and then again last year. Restrictions lasted until almost December after the warmest spring since 1910 and the lowest rainfall since 1976.

Temperatures have risen higher this year, with the warmest spring and hottest June on record. No rain has fallen this month in Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire and West Sussex, and 16 counties have recorded 0.1mm, according to the Met Office.

North Wales and the Upper Severn became the first part of the UK to declare a drought last week. Temperatures in the South are expected to climb again this week in what may be the fourth official heatwave of the year so far.

Emergency services are also braced for further wildfires. Blazes along a stretch of the WCML near Winsford, Cheshire, closed Europe’s busiest intercity rail route in both directions this month, leading to more than 70 trains being cancelled. Sparks from a passing steam train were blamed for the incident.

Commuters across much of Britain were advised not to travel during June’s sweltering temperatures as the heat and direct sunlight caused rails to expand and buckle.

Hot weather is one phenomenon slowing down Britain’s trains. Leaves on the line, which can cause trains to skid, remain a perennial problem. The issue has led to programmes of mass felling and the deployment of special trains to apply sand to tracks in problem areas, with the aim of helping wheels gain a better grip.

data.title: Taxpayer-owned British Steel owes China £1bn
data.description:
Taxpayer-owned British Steel owed almost £1bn to its former Chinese owners when it was nationalised by Labour, newly published accounts showed.

The Government formally took ownership of the struggling business last month in a move aimed at protecting jobs and keeping the blast furnaces going at its site in Scunthorpe, Lincolnshire.

But recent accounts reveal the scale of liabilities taxpayers face as a result, including substantial debts owed by the loss-making company alongside ongoing operational costs.

These include at least £960m that British Steel owed to Jingye, its former Chinese parent, in the form of intercompany loans at the end of 2024.

Jingye is expected to pursue that sum as compensation and has already begun proceedings under an existing UK-China investment treaty.

The accounts also suggest that simply keeping British Steel afloat will be a costly endeavour in itself.

The document, signed off by Jingye just days before the company was nationalised, says a fresh funding injection of “£275m to £330m” will be needed “over the next 12 months” alone. The Treasury has already provided some £555m of working capital to the business.

At the same time, British Steel’s physical assets – including property, plant and equipment – have been deemed largely worthless after an audit review.

The company, which employs 2,700 workers, cannot produce steel profitably. British Steel reported sales of £829m in 2024, but made a loss of £254m. This was equivalent to a loss of £201 per tonne of steel, before taxes, the accounts said.

Liquid steel production also fell by nearly a quarter to 1.3 million tonnes after the business suffered “severe and persistent operational problems” in 2024.

These included periods where only one furnace was available, as well as several “chill” events, where blast furnaces failed to sustain the heat required for production.

The furnaces were so unstable that on several occasions steel was deemed too poor quality to be used, the documents said.

One industry source likened the company to a “money pit”, adding: “The longer they keep the blast furnaces open, the longer they are going to lose money hand over fist.

“Obviously, closure is pretty unpalatable from a political point of view though. It’s also hard to imagine anyone being very happy about giving money to Jingye.”

The Government first seized operational control of British Steel in April 2025 from ‌Jingye after ministers became concerned that the Chinese company was seeking to irreversibly close the blast furnaces.

This was primarily based on a belief that the company was failing to buy enough raw materials to keep them going – a claim that Jingye denies.

Parliament later passed a bill that allowed ministers to take formal ownership of the plant in the public interest, which took effect in July this year.

That bill also required the Government to consider what compensation, if any, was payable to Jingye.

It is understood that this process, which will begin in the autumn and be overseen by an independent valuer, could determine that no money is ultimately due.

The decision by the former Starmer premiership to nationalise the company triggered a backlash from Beijing, which said it was “strongly dissatisfied” at the time.

A government spokesman said on Thursday: “After assessing the impact on our economy, critical national infrastructure and national security, we concluded that public ownership was the best way to secure British Steel’s future and protect the future of UK steel production.

“An independent valuer would determine what, if any, is payable to Jingye, and our focus is now on stabilising the business, backing the communities that rely on it and building a sustainable, competitive and decarbonised steel sector for the years ahead.”

data.title: S&P 500 closes at record high as employers cut 23,000 jobs
data.description:
The S&P 500 closed at a record high on Friday after the US government reported that employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month.

Every major index saw a second straight week of gains, which included several fresh records. It marks a strong start to August following several weak months.

The S&P 500 rose 47.68 points, or 0.6pc, to 7,757.64, topping the all-time high it set on Tuesday. The benchmark index has been on a record run throughout the year.

The bond market reacted more strongly to the weaker signal on the jobs market, which can be seen as allowing the Federal Reserve more time before raising interest rates to fight inflation.

Technology stocks, with their big market values, did much of the heavy lifting for the broader market. They are often the heaviest weights determining the market’s direction. Nvidia jumped 2.3pc and Broadcom rose 1.7pc.

It comes as one of Britain’s biggest AI companies is planning to float in New York in a new blow to London’s hopes of attracting tech listings.

London-based data centre company Nscale is preparing for a US initial public offering as soon as next month.

Nscale is targeting New York despite receiving vocal support from the UK Government. The move would prolong the struggles of the London Stock Exchange in attracting tech companies to list.

The company did not comment on its IPO plans.

The flotation could value Nscale, run by the Australian former cryptocurrency miner Josh Payne, at around $25bn (£19bn), according to tech news website The Information.

Founded two years ago, Nscale has former Facebook luminaries Sir Nick Clegg and Sheryl Sandberg on its board.

Nscale is touting potential contracts worth $51bn to entice investors ahead of the flotation, according to Bloomberg, although revenue in the second quarter was around $100m. While the flotation could be as early as September, the timeline could slip.

British tech companies including semiconductor giant Arm have chosen to list in the US instead of London.

Nscale, whose investors include Nvidia and Dell, recently raised $2bn in what was Europe’s biggest ever “series C”, or third stage, funding round.

If Nscale follows through with plans to go public in the US, it risks embarrassment for the Government.

Labour has championed the company as a centrepiece of Britain’s AI boom. Mr Payne has described his company as “the only full stack sovereign AI infrastructure provider in the UK”.

Lord Stockwood, the former investment minister, put pressure on local councillors to approve a “supercomputer” data centre being built by the company in Essex, saying the matter was a priority for former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, said in March that Nscale’s funding was “in part as a result of the Government’s support and convening”.

The company has appeared to be preparing for a US flotation for some time. It hired Wall Street banker Alice Takhtajan, who had worked on a string of New York flotations, as its chief financial officer in December.

Company documents also contain references to registering securities under US stock market legislation.

Despite its London headquarters, only one of the four data centres it is building is based in Britain. Two are in Norway and one in the US. A project with OpenAI for a “Stargate” facility in the North East was put on hold earlier this year after OpenAI criticised Britain’s high energy costs.

Nscale said this week that it was doubling office space in London.

A string of so-called AI infrastructure companies have listed in the US in recent years including Coreweave and Nebius amid booming demand from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: John Lewis boss warns of ‘really tough’ trading
data.description:
The boss of John Lewis has warned retailers are facing “really tough” trading conditions that threaten to undermine the department store’s turnaround.

Jason Tarry, the chairman of the John Lewis Partnership, which also owns Waitrose, told staff the retailer had been forced to “trade into lower sales and higher costs” in recent months.

In an interview for the company’s internal magazine, Mr Tarry said John Lewis needed to “adjust for an immediate future that we weren’t expecting even six months ago, let alone a couple of years ago”.

He said the retailer was “heavily focused at the moment on what that means for us in terms of adjusting our plan going forward”. The remarks were first reported by the Financial Times.

Mr Tarry joined John Lewis as chairman two years ago after more than three decades at Tesco, replacing Dame Sharon White, the former boss.

Retailers have been grappling with cost increases as the conflict in Iran hit supply chains, while higher fuel prices and inflationary pressures have pushed consumers to tighten their belts.

In financial results published earlier this year, John Lewis fell to a £21m pre-tax loss in 2025 compared with a pre-tax profit of £97m a year prior. The retailer also cut around 3,300 jobs last year, according to its annual report.

Since then, it has launched a further redundancy consultation across dozens of stores as it cuts foreign exchange services and gift-wrapping desks as part of a cost-cutting drive.

It has also told staff they must be in the office more often as it races to keep up with rivals who have increasingly ditched remote working.

As part of his turnaround plan, Mr Tarry has focused the group’s strategy on its core retail businesses, abandoning his predecessor’s plan to build thousands of rental homes.

Instead, he has laid out plans to reinvest in its stores, including by opening new Waitrose shops and refurbishing existing ones.

In the interview, Mr Tarry said staff should not expect the pace of change to slow down during his tenure.

“My honest counsel to anyone asking when it will end is that it will never end,” he said.

A John Lewis spokesman said: “It’s no secret that trading conditions are challenging right now as people think carefully about their spending.

“Our priority is to do the right thing for our customers so we’re continuing to invest significantly in our brands with new and refurbished Waitrose shops and fresh propositions in John Lewis like our new beauty and sports halls and Platter hospitality offer.”

Separately on Wednesday, Next reported that its sales for the last quarter were well ahead of expectations, sending shares to a new record high.

The retailer, led by Lord Wolfson, reported a 9.2pc increase in full-price sales over the quarter and said its profits for the year would be higher than previously forecast. Next said the summer heatwave had helped drive a boost in clothing sales.

data.title: Buyers face £55,000 in ‘hidden’ cost on new homes
data.description:
Buyers face paying £55,000 in “hidden” costs when they purchase a new-build home, fresh calculations suggest.

Taxes placed on housebuilders to fund initiatives such as affordable housing and net zero policies are not being divulged to homebuyers when they buy properties, according to a policy analyst.

Alan Hibben, who writes for the Centre for Policy Studies, estimates that a typical £450,000 new-build home in southern England has £55,000 of “hidden” costs included in the price.

These include £10,000 for so-called “biodiversity net gain”, a rule in England that requires most builders to make wildlife habitats at least 10pc richer than before construction began.

A further £30,000 is paid by housebuilders for “planning obligations”, which help fund affordable housing and local roads.

The rest is comprised of planning fees and the cost of planning delays.

However, stamp duty, which would be £10,000 for a £450,000 property, is the only tax which buyers would see when they view their invoice.

Mr Hibben said his calculations showed the “hidden nature of these costs and the impact of policy decisions on affordability”.

“Policy objectives for the country as a whole are being put on the backs of home buyers, rather than general taxation, so that the costs can be hidden and builders to blame, rather than politicians,” he said.

He said the UK should copy Canada and show buyers all the taxes they are paying.

“Successive British governments have done the opposite: they have buried new taxes, fees and charges inside other systems, especially planning,” he said.

“The result is a housing market in which public-policy costs are embedded in the price of a home, while political debate proceeds as if buyers were paying only for land, labour and materials.”

Since the Iran war began, mortgage rates have climbed, prolonging a slowdown in the housing market as prospective buyers hold off on purchasing a home.

On top of weakening demand, housebuilders are also contending with higher build costs, rising taxes, delays from the planning system and strict regulations.

These factors have pushed up the cost of building a new home by £76,000 since 2020, according to the Home Builders Federation.

Housing construction improved slightly in July, according to the latest S&P Global UK construction purchasing managers’ index, but remains firmly in contraction.

Any reading above 50 shows an increase in activity, while anything below shows construction is contracting.

data.title: Bake Off bun fight triggers legal battle at Sky
data.description:
A former boss of The Great British Bake Off is suing Sky amid claims the broadcaster attempted to poach the show from Channel 4.

Letty Kavanagh, who helped make the show, claims she was fired for raising concerns about the programme’s future after Sky allegedly tried to acquire the rights to Bake Off and remove it from terrestrial TV.

Bake Off has been broadcast on Channel 4 since 2017 despite being made by Sky’s Love Productions subsidiary.

Sky is understood to have wanted the show for its own networks when Channel 4’s broadcast deal came up for renewal in 2024, although it was unsuccessful in acquiring the programme.

However, Ms Kavanagh reportedly alleged that Sky’s pursuit of the TV show was itself a conflict of interest, since – through its ownership of Love Productions – it was aware of contractual arrangements with Channel 4.

She also alleged that Sky planned to cancel some of the show’s spin-offs, such as the celebrity version and Junior Bake Off.

She reportedly claimed that this would have put hundreds of jobs at risk and would have damaged Bake Off’s brand, according to Deadline, which first reported the claims.

Ms Kavanagh has filed a legal claim at the High Court for breach of contract against Sky and Love Productions. Sky has disputed the allegation, arguing that there is no legal basis for the claim.

The Great British Bake Off is one of Britain’s most popular TV shows.

Originally broadcast on the BBC, the inaugural presenters were Mel Giedroyc and Sue Perkins, both comedians, with Paul Hollywood and Dame Mary Berry as judges.

The Channel 4 version saw Noel Fielding and Sandi Toksvig take the helm as presenters with Dame Prue Leith judging alongside Mr Hollywood.

Love Productions will soon have a new owner after Sky agreed to hand the maker of The Great British Bake Off to ITV as part of a £1.6bn mega-deal. 

ITV Studios will become a standalone production business and has secured a £2.1bn commitment with Sky for five years for shows including Coronation Street, Emmerdale, Love Island and I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!.

As part of the deal, it was announced that ITV Studios would acquire Love Productions for £200m, meaning the Bake Off producer will have a new owner.

Bake Off will return for its 17th season next month and Nigella Lawson will replace Dame Prue as a judge on the baking competition series.

A Sky spokesman said: “We do not recognise Ms Kavanagh’s account of events. We reject the possibility of a conflict of interest in relation to assets we control and wholly own and refute her allegations of discrimination and retaliation in the strongest possible terms.

“We do not intend to comment further at this stage. Regrettably, this matter is the subject of ongoing legal proceedings, in which we intend to vigorously defend our position.”

Love Productions and Ms Kavanagh’s lawyers were contacted for comment.

data.title: Raleigh’s downfall is an indictment of British manufacturing
data.description:
With famous models such as the Grifter, the Burner and, perhaps most of all, the Chopper, Raleigh remains one of the most treasured brands in cycling history.

Older readers will recall the latter fondly as one of the most wished-for Christmas gifts of the 1970s.

And yet this week we learned that Accell, the Dutch owner of the bike manufacturer, has filed for insolvency.

Sure, companies run into trouble all the time. And yet, the long and painful decline of Raleigh is surely emblematic of everything that has gone wrong with British manufacturing in the last 50 years – and unfortunately there is not much point in talking about building new industries if we can’t keep the old ones alive.

In some parallel universe, Raleigh might be a huge success. After all, it is not as if cycling isn’t popular.

Indeed, in most British cities you can hardly cross the street without a few bikers whizzing past you. Around 17pc of us cycle regularly, while in countries such as the Netherlands it is more than 50pc.

The global market is worth an estimated $35bn (£26bn), and it is growing at 6pc-plus every year. Put simply, this is an industry where there is plenty of money to be made.

And yet, to put it mildly, none of that has helped Raleigh.

Traced back to a small Nottingham workshop in 1885, the company grew into the world’s largest bicycle maker by 1913, retaining that crown for decades. It was synonymous with reliable, simple transport and one of the major employers in the East Midlands.

In the past 50 years, however, it has been a sad tale of relentless decline. It was taken over by the largely forgotten industrial conglomerate Tube Investments (TI), before falling into the hands of the German-owned Derby Cycles, and finally that of Accell from the Netherlands.

Production here in Britain ended more than 20 years ago, and now its latest owner has filed for insolvency.

Perhaps someone else will buy out the branding rights from the administrators. Or perhaps they won’t.

We will find out in the next few weeks, but whatever happens, it is hard to see Raleigh surviving as anything more than a badge – and perhaps not even that.

This keeps happening. Denby Pottery, another brand with a great heritage, appointed administrators earlier this year, and stopped production after 200 years.

Liberty Steel has closed, and most of what remains of the industry has been nationalised.

It is hard to believe that Jaguar Land Rover will be with us much longer, given how many mistakes the company has made, or its enthusiasm for trashing a brand that was once one of the best in the global market for upmarket cars. The list goes on.

All the major developed economies struggle to stay competitive in manufacturing, given the rise of first Japanese and now Chinese rivals. But Britain struggles more than most.

There is no other major country that has lost so many key industries so completely as we have. The result?

We have already dropped out of the top 10 global manufacturing nations, overtaken by the likes of Mexico and even Russia, and we show little sign of recovering our place among the world’s leaders any time soon.

We need to learn the lessons of that. The UK has been for too long a brutal place to run a manufacturing business.

It started with the trade union militancy of the 1960s and 1970s, which made it harder and harder for the likes of Raleigh to remain competitive, first with the rest of Europe and then with Asia.

The industrial conglomerates of the 1980s may have briefly stopped some of the rot, but conglomerates such as TI, or rivals such as Hanson and BTR, lacked the expertise or ambition to grow the brands they controlled – and have since mostly disappeared.

As this century has unfolded, it has become even worse, with punishingly high energy prices and green levies that could have been purposely designed to make it as hard as possible to produce anything in a factory. It has been a long downward trend, with only brief pauses on the way.

The new Government led by Andy Burnham talks a lot about reviving manufacturing and creating new industries. But what is the point if we can’t keep the ones we already have alive?

There is not much hope of dominating solar power or microchips or space launchers – or whatever the latest Business Secretary has decided will generate the right kind of headlines this week – if we can’t make a bike. We are just kidding ourselves. It is not going to happen.

It doesn’t have to be impossible. We need far lower corporate taxes; much cheaper industrial energy; more flexible labour rules; an end to planning restrictions that make it virtually impossible to expand plants in the right place; better infrastructure; trade deals that allow access to the biggest markets on fair terms; and welfare reforms that make it possible to find people to do the jobs that are needed if a business happens to start growing again.

There is nothing very complicated about it. With the right mix, more companies would survive and might actually start growing again.

But right now there is very little sign that the new Government, for all its rhetoric about helping the North – or actually the East Midlands in this case – understands what is needed any more than the last few did.

There are probably plenty of teenagers, who already have vinyl collections and VHS players, who would like to find a retro Chopper under the Christmas tree, and parents who would pay handsomely for it, especially if it had the authenticity of being “Made in Nottingham”.

But it is not going to happen. Raleigh’s long decline is a sorry tale of industrial incompetence, and unfortunately it looks as if there is little sign of that ending any time soon.

data.title: Debt-laden TalkTalk offloads customers in scramble to raise funds
data.description:
TalkTalk has offloaded swathes of customers to a start-up rival as it scrambles to raise cash.

The deal to sell 120,000 customers to fledgling provider Rise Fibre marks the latest effort by the debt-ridden broadband provider to shore up its balance sheet.

Terms of the sale were not disclosed.

It comes as the broadband firm, which was founded by Sir Charles Dunstone, struggles under a £1.4bn debt pile.

TalkTalk secured a £115m lifeline from Ares Management and other shareholders, including £65m in fresh debt, earlier this year.

This was less than 12 months after backers were forced to provide a £235m emergency bailout to avoid a looming debt default.

The deal with Rise Fibre marks the latest whittling down of TalkTalk’s customer base after it reached an agreement to sell 29,000 subscribers to Utility Warehouse for £5m earlier this year.

While the deals have raised much-needed cash for the business, they have fuelled questions over the prospect of TalkTalk finding a buyer for the remainder of its consumer division.

James Ratzer, an analyst at New Street Research, said: “The more these piecemeal customer disposals occur and the organic TalkTalk consumer base shrinks further, the size of the remaining base decreases further and will therefore continue to raise the question of whether it becomes possible to consider an acquisition of the whole of TalkTalk consumer.”

TalkTalk is separately exploring a sale of its wholesale division, called Platform X.

VodafoneThree is understood to have tabled a bid for the division alongside several private equity firms. TalkTalk has previously said that the break-up will be completed by the end of summer.

However, figures released to investors this week show TalkTalk’s underlying business is still struggling as it cuts back heavily on costs.

Revenues fell by 15pc in the first three months of the financial year to £292m as the company’s retail customer base dropped to 1.6 million – down by a quarter on last year.

TalkTalk burned through another £58m in cash over the quarter, highlighting the strain on its balance sheet.

The financial pressures have previously caused TalkTalk to fall behind on payments to suppliers including Openreach, BT’s network division.

Bosses were forced last year to secure a letter of credit from one of its lenders to guarantee £73m owed to Openreach.

However, TalkTalk said its interest bill was now lower after reaching an agreement with its lenders, while it had also cut spending thanks to cost-cutting measures.

The deal with Rise Fibre, which predominantly covers customers on CityFibre’s network, will more than double the broadband challenger’s subscriber base to almost 250,000.

The Manchester-based company was spun out of alt-net 4th Utility a year ago. It uses 4th Utility’s network as well as those of rivals including BT’s Openreach and CityFibre.

Rise Fibre, which is backed by the infrastructure arm of private equity firm CVC, has set out a target of reaching one million customers.

Steve Wilson, the chief executive of Rise Fibre, said: “This is far more than an acquisition. It marks another major step in the emergence of a genuine new challenger in UK broadband.

“We have ambitious plans to continue growing through further acquisitions and strong organic performance as we build the UK’s fastest-growing broadband provider.”

TalkTalk declined to comment.

A current account is a transactional account that typically pays no interest but gives you a lot of flexibility in how often you access your money.

data.title: North Sea shutdown to cost Treasury billions in tax relief
data.description:
The Treasury faces a multibillion-pound hit from Labour’s North Sea shutdown, BP’s former finance chief has warned.

Brian Gilvary, who sat on the board of BP from 2012 to 2020, said punishing tax rates and a ban on new drilling had prompted many oil and gas operators to halt activity in British waters sooner than expected.

As a result, companies are ripping pipes and platforms out of the sea far earlier than planned. The vast costs of such decommissioning can be claimed back against the tax paid on previous years’ profits, meaning a huge rebate bill for the Treasury.

The latest estimates suggest the rebates, plus foregone tax from North Sea operations, could cost the Treasury around £13bn between now and 2035.

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Gilvary, who is now chairman of Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Energy, said: “Forcing fields to close prematurely does not simply switch off future tax receipts; it also brings forward the point at which those decommissioning tax reliefs crystallise, increasing the near-term pressure on the public finances.”

Mr Gilvary said the decline of the UK oil and gas industry under Labour was “eroding long-term national wealth” and damaging “the fiscal capacity to fund public services”.

The warning comes a week after BP announced plans to exit the North Sea by selling its operations there. Meg O’Neill, the company’s chief executive, has since said the region “doesn’t compete for capital”.

Oil and gas companies face a 78pc levy on their UK profits after Labour increased a windfall tax on the industry when it came to power. The Government has also extended the levy by two years, from 2028 to 2030.

Mr Gilvary said BP’s decision to exit the North Sea was “a tangible warning sign” about the cost of these policies.

He said: “When major operators retreat, the consequences ripple far beyond corporate balance sheets.

“Investment falls, supply chains weaken, and highly skilled jobs, many clustered in Scotland and the North East, begin to disappear. Tax revenues decline, and with them the fiscal capacity to fund public services and the energy transition itself.”

Annual decommissioning costs have already risen from £2bn in 2024, the year of Labour’s election, to £3bn every year from now to at least 2030, according to data from industry regulator the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA).

Labour’s ‘folly’

The NSTA predicts at least £28bn will be spent on shutting down the North Sea from now to 2035. This implies a total cost to the Treasury of around £13bn over that period.

Ashley Kelty, an oil and gas analyst at investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “This shows the folly of the drive to shut down the North Sea.

“Another risk that ministers fail to appreciate is that closing down some of the key offshore hubs will leave other fields stranded and also forced to close. It means the basin closes down even faster, with less tax generated and more relief having to be given.”

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has signalled that he will soften Labour’s stance on oil and gas, saying the UK “cannot ignore” North Sea resources.

A key test of his resolve will be on Jackdaw and Rosebank, two large oil and gas projects awaiting approval. A consultation on Jackdaw ends on Monday. It has the potential to deliver around 6pc of the UK’s gas supply, or enough to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes, according to operator Adura.

In total, the NSTA estimates it will cost about £48bn to decommission all operations in the North Sea. It suggests the final tax rebate bill for the Treasury will approach £30bn.

Others believe even this is a huge underestimate. A National Audit Office report in 2019 said that total North Sea decommissioning costs could be as high as £77bn, or about £101bn in today’s money.

A government spokesman said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security.

“Our focus is on providing stability and supporting North Sea workers and communities as they continue to make a vital contribution to the UK’s economy.”

We must stop paying other countries for energy we can produce ourselves

By Brian Gilvary

The UK is making a strategic error in the North Sea, one that risks undermining energy security, destroying high-value jobs and eroding long-term national wealth.

At the heart of the problem is policy instability. The Energy Profits Levy (EPL), or windfall tax, combined with an effective ban on new drilling, has sent a clear signal to investors: the UK is no longer a reliable place to deploy capital.

Predictably, capital has gone elsewhere.

Nowhere is that more evident than in Norway, where investment in the continental shelf is running at roughly 10 times UK levels.

Even more perversely, Norway is exporting gas to the UK, from the same basin, energy we could in part produce ourselves, while British consumers and taxpayers absorb the cost.

This is not an abstract concern. BP’s decision to scale back and sell North Sea assets is a tangible warning sign. When major operators retreat, the consequences ripple far beyond corporate balance sheets. Investment falls, supply chains weaken, and highly skilled jobs, many clustered in Scotland and the North East, begin to disappear. Tax revenues decline, and with them the fiscal capacity to fund public services and the energy transition itself.

There is a further, often overlooked cost to the Exchequer. Companies can offset a significant proportion of North Sea decommissioning costs against tax, reducing the overall cost of removing platforms and plugging wells.

With the North Sea Transition Authority estimating that around £44bn remains to be spent on decommissioning, the Exchequer faces billions of pounds in tax relief over the coming decades.

Forcing fields to close prematurely does not simply switch off future tax receipts; it also brings forward the point at which those decommissioning tax reliefs crystallise, increasing the near-term pressure on the public finances.

The uncomfortable truth is that UK demand for oil and gas has not vanished. Instead, we are increasingly choosing to import what we could produce domestically, often with a higher carbon footprint. That is not climate leadership; it is carbon leakage combined with economic self-harm.

Union leaders have been blunt about the stakes. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, has warned that “without a coherent plan for domestic energy, we risk sacrificing tens of thousands of skilled jobs and hollowing out entire industrial communities”. Similarly, the GMB has stressed that “North Sea workers should not be collateral damage in a poorly managed transition” and called for sustained investment in domestic production alongside the growth of renewables.

This is not a fringe view. Even those strongly committed to climate action recognise the need for balance. Sir Tony Blair recently cautioned that “people feel they are being asked to make financial sacrifices and changes in lifestyle when they know the impact on global emissions is minimal”, arguing for a more pragmatic approach that protects economic resilience while pursuing decarbonisation.

The UK still has significant remaining reserves in the North Sea. With the right fiscal framework, these resources can be developed responsibly, supporting jobs, strengthening energy security and generating revenues to fund the transition to cleaner energy systems. The alternative – continued policy volatility and punitive taxation – will accelerate decline without reducing demand.

Reversing course requires two clear steps.

First, the Government should remove or substantially reform the Energy Profits Levy to restore investor confidence and create a stable, predictable fiscal regime.

Second, it should lift restrictions on new drilling, allowing companies to invest in projects that can deliver domestic supply over the coming decades.

This is ultimately a question of choice. The UK can either manage the decline of the North Sea in a way that maximises economic value and energy security, or it can force a premature contraction that benefits competitors, increases imports and weakens the domestic economy.

A credible energy strategy must recognise that oil and gas will remain part of the UK’s energy mix for years to come. The question is not whether we use these resources, but whether we produce them ourselves, or pay others to do it.

Brian Gilvary is the chairman of Ineos Energy

data.title: Barclays in legal fight over collapsed shadow bank’s cash
data.description:
Barclays is facing a legal battle over cash held in accounts belonging to a collapsed shadow bank.

Administrators for Market Financial Solutions (MFS) have filed a case at the High Court in an attempt to force Barclays to hand over money they believe is owed to the business.

AlixPartners, the administrators, were appointed to oversee parts of MFS by some of the shadow bank’s creditors just before it collapsed amid allegations of fraud earlier this year.

It is understood that Barclays will be defending the case.  It is believed that Barclays was holding more than £160m belonging to various parts of the MFS business at the time it collapsed into administration. 

Barclays provided bank accounts to MFS and most of its associated lending vehicles. It also lent money to the collapsed shadow bank, meaning it stands to lose out from the collapse.

The bank has said that its total exposure to MFS amounted to around £500m. However, it expects to recover more than 50pc of that.

A number of administrators acting on behalf of different MFS creditors have claimed Barclays has refused to hand over cash held in bank accounts.

MFS was a shadow bank, which meant it did not accept deposits and instead funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders including Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies.

Begbies Traynor and Coots & Boots, which are acting for other creditors of MFS, said Barclays had refused to transfer credit balances it believed were owed to them.

The administrators said Barclays argued this was because of widespread allegations of fraud against MFS, associated freezing orders over certain parties involved in the case and claims that the bank may itself have over the funds.

Grant Thornton successfully applied to the High Court in May to force Barclays to hand over £21.1m held in a bank account controlled by an MFS vehicle.

The lender collapsed into administration in February, prompting allegations that at least £1.3bn had been “misappropriated” from the business.

Paresh Raja, the company’s founder, has been accused of “plundering” MFS to fund a lavish lifestyle.

Mr Raja and his wife allegedly received more than £408m from “funds managed by MFS” to “personal bank accounts” in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates.

Mr Raja strongly denies the allegations and has consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

AlixPartners successfully obtained a freezing order against Mr Raja in March, preventing him from spending more than £5,000 a week without the consent of MFS’s administrators.

Barclays’ relationship with MFS dated back at least 15 years.

The Telegraph revealed earlier this year that MFS paid off millions of pounds owed to Barclays by borrowing from other banks before it plunged into administration.

While some of these deals were going on, Barclays was already in the process of shutting MFS’s bank accounts.

Its failure to warn other banks that lent to MFS has angered fellow creditors and raised questions about what exactly it knew about the collapsed shadow bank.

Barclays and AlixPartners declined to comment.

data.title: Bank tax raid would hurt Britain, Wall Street chief warns Burnham
data.description:
A fresh tax raid on banks would hurt Britain, the boss of one of Wall Street’s biggest banks has warned Andy Burnham.

Dame Jane Fraser, the Scottish-born chief executive of Citigroup investment bank, said that any increase in taxes risked making the UK a prohibitively expensive place to do business.

During a visit to London on Wednesday, she said that “money moves with its feet”, pointing out that “even Frankfurt and Paris are lower” when it comes to taxes for banks.

“It makes it a tougher decision. You know, it’s already one of the most expensive centres in the world,” she added.

Dame Jane signalled that customers may choose to do business elsewhere should the Prime Minister raise taxes on banks.

“When your clients have a lot of choices to where things get booked, we have to make choices to where things get booked,” she said. “If the taxes go up even higher then that makes it an easier decision not to book it in London.”

Banks face the usual 25pc rate of tax charged on companies’ profits, plus an extra corporation tax supplement of 3pc.

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) has been lobbying Labour to increase this bank surcharge to as high as 35pc, a move it claims could raise £60bn.

Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, has called for the surcharge to increase to 5pc, according to a Cabinet memo revealed by The Telegraph last year.

Dame Jane said: “In the UK, we need growth and we need competitiveness. And our strongest competitive capability here is our capital market. Don’t undermine it.

“I grew up at one point when the Labour Party had a 105pc tax rate in the lae Seventies and it was a disaster for the country and you don’t grow and you don’t build businesses and other pieces.

“I think there’s a balance but there’s also some tough choices. We cannot afford everything here that we would like to pay for. So being realistic about that and having a sensible fiscal policy that the market finds palatable is going to be very important.”

The banking sector is estimated to have paid £43.3bn in taxes to the UK Government last year, up by a third since 2014.

A report by UK Finance last year estimated that the total tax rate for banks was 46.4pc once other levies such as VAT and National Insurance were factored in.

That is higher than Amsterdam and Frankfurt – at 42.2pc and 38.9pc, respectively – and well above either Dublin or New York, where total tax takes are both below 30pc.

Mr Burnham’s Government has given no indication as to whether it would raise taxes on banks. However, the Prime Minister has signalled that he was considering tax rises.

The UK’s fiscal situation remains extremely delicate. In March, Rachel Reeves had breathing space of just over £23bn between her tax receipts and spending plans.

However, since then the Government has been hit by headwinds from the war in Iran and higher fuel costs have put pressure on inflation and interest rates.

Dame Jane is the latest senior bank boss to warn Britain against increasing the burden on the sector.

Last month, Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan, said there would be “adverse consequences” if Mr Burnham targeted lenders with higher taxes.

The bosses of Barclays, NatWest and HSBC have issued similar warnings in recent weeks.

Dame Jane said: “We care about the UK. This is a very important centre for Citi and I don’t want to see London diminished.”

She said that London remained the bank’s most important financial centre outside of the US. Citi has invested $1.5bn (£1.1bn) into the redevelopment of its London headquarters in Canary Wharf, which is expected to open soon.

A Treasury spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities: to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode.

“As has always been the case, the Chancellor will set out decisions at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: Kent seaside towns’ water supplies ‘critically low’
data.description:
Tourist hotspots in Kent are on the brink of losing their water supplies as half the country grapples with drought.

South East Water told residents in Whitstable and Herne Bay on the Kent coast and Charing further inland that they should only use water for drinking, washing and cooking because storage was “critically low”.

The utility said: “Urgent message for customers in Charing, Whitstable and Herne Bay. Storage tanks in your area are critically low. You may lose supply unless demand for water in the area drops low enough for the tanks to refill.

“Please continue to only use water for drinking, cooking and hygiene.”

A South East Water spokesman said it had completed “precautionary bottled water deliveries” to properties in Charing and was monitoring water supplies in Herne Bay and Whitstable.

The spokesman said: “If the situation escalates, we will then look to set up bottled water stations and complete wider deliveries of bottled water.”

The three towns have a combined population of more than 75,000 people.

The Environment Agency declared half of England in drought last week, following record-low rainfall and extremely high temperatures.

Alistair Carmichael, the head of the environment committee, said: “This news is as unsurprising as it will be unwelcome for the long suffering customers of South East Water.

“There is clearly little resilience in their operation and that is not going to change overnight, although the new management team need to be coming up soon with a plan for that.”

Matthew Dean, the incident manager for South East Water, said water levels in its storage tank for the three areas were extremely low “due to the prolonged period of hot and dry weather”.

Mr Dean said: “All customers are currently in supply. However, if demand for water continues to remain high, there is a risk of supply interruptions.

“To safeguard our shared resource and help prevent any homes from facing a sudden loss of water, we are incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies in Kent.”

It is a fresh blow for South East Water, which provides water to 2.3 million customers across Kent, Surrey, Sussex, Berkshire and Hampshire.

The company, which has £1.7bn of debt, struck a deal last month for £200m of funding to help keep it afloat.

It was fined £30m in July for supply interruptions that left 70,000 homes in the Kent town of Tunbridge Wells without water.

Roughly 40pc of England’s population is under a hosepipe ban along with parts of Wales, imposed by nine water companies.

There have been four record-breaking heatwaves so far this summer, stoking wildfires across Britain and jeopardising swathes of farmland.

data.title: Rod Liddle, Today programme editor turned polemical journalist with an army of devoted readers
data.description:
​​Rod Liddle, who has died aged 66, was arguably the most offensive columnist of his generation in the British press – and wore that badge with pride. To his army of devoted readers he was also the funniest, and the first to burst every balloon of political cant, self-proclaimed victimhood and Left-liberal pomposity.

Liddle’s career as a controversialist was launched by his forced resignation, in 2003, from the role of editor of Radio 4’s Today programme. A column he had written for The Guardian, in which he mocked pro-hunting Countryside Alliance marchers as “rather angry, ruddy-faced people”, was deemed to breach BBC impartiality rules.

Thereafter, in the pages of The Spectator, The Sunday Times and The Sun, and on the airwaves, he took on all-comers, from the commissars of correctness in the broadcast media to the panjandrums of the race-relations industry and the increasingly strident advocates of transgender rights.

Objects of his ad hominem derision ranged ​from the Labour government’s equalities champion Harriet Harman – to whom he eventually apologised for an attack that began “So – Harriet Harman, then. Would you? I mean after a few beers obviously, not while you were sober” – to the rabble-rousing imam of Finsbury Park, Abu Hamza, who had lost both hands in an explosion and to whom Liddle habitually referred as “Hookie”.

Many of his sharpest barbs were aimed at what he saw as the self-reinforcing networks of the “faux Leftie” liberal elite, whose members filled any number of powerful committees and boards, thereby largely controlling the parameters of public debate on issues that animated Liddle. He dubbed this phenomenon “Six Degrees of Shami” in reference to Shami (now Baroness) Chakraba​rti, the ubiquitous civil liberties campaigner turned shadow Labour minister.

He especially loathed members of that elite who let slip their contempt for the white working class, whom Liddle himself felt had been left behind by social change, bad education and modern obsessions with multiculturalism and minority rights. In this respect he singled out the Independent columnist Yasmin Alibhai-Brown – who gave as good as she got, telling Liddle in a heated Channel 4 debate that she loathed him and was proud to say so to his face.

The truth about Liddle was that he possessed a formidable journalistic nose for hypocrisy and lies, but that he could also be loose with his facts and hurtful with his epithets, particularly when feeling crapulous and close to deadline – leading to several referrals to the Press Complaints Commission and many occasions when he had to defend himself against accusations of racism, homophobia, transphobia and other contemporary thought crimes.

Loyal readers, however, knew where he was really coming from and recognised the dark picture he painted. In particular they understood his sympathy for the common man who had been abandoned by politicians and become a target of casual media scorn.

This instinct was never better expressed than in a 2006 column in which he tracked down, in their Newbury council house, the mother and father of a 14-year-old drink-driver who had kicked off violently in court while her parents hurled eggs at the assembled media: what he found was a couple “perpetually on their uppers”, but kind, loyal and doing their best for their family – an echo, perhaps, of the humble upbringing that was the fount of all his writings.

Roderick Edwin Liddle was born at Sidcup, Kent, on April 1 1960, the son of Edwin Liddle and his wife Margaret, née Clee. Edwin’s father Joseph, from Darlington, had been an engine driver; Edwin worked for the railways and did war service in motor torpedo boats before becoming an Inland Revenue clerk.

When Rod was eight the family moved to Nunthorpe, a “select” suburb of Middlesbrough (though he wrote that describing it thus was a little like saying “a select area of Mogadishu”), where he was educated at Laurence Jackson comprehensive and Prior Pursglove sixth-form college, formed a punk band and joined the Socialist Workers Party.

“I was at my best when I was 16 or 17,” he recalled, “energetic but obnoxious.” He also recalled his long-suffering father’s comment on seeing him dressed for a night on the town, earring in one ear, ripped trousers with “Fuck Off” written on them in Magic Marker, bright red SWP badge on the lapel of a filthy secondhand jacket: “Christ, you can’t sink any bloody lower.”

Having entered journalism as a reporter on the South Wales Echo, Liddle worked for the Labour Party as a speechwriter and researcher from 1983 to 1987 and went on to study social psychology as a mature student at the LSE before joining the BBC as a trainee producer. Appointed editor of Today in 1998, he boosted the programme’s reputation for investigative journalism, winning a number of awards.

After he left Today Liddle enjoyed a brief foray into light entertainment as a team captain opposite Alan Coren on Call My Bluff, but his style of humour proved too saturnine. In 2003 he published a collection of short stories, Too Beautiful for You, and in 2007 a satirical novel, Love Will Destroy Everything.

His non-fiction work Selfish, Whining Monkeys: How We Ended Up Greedy, Narcissistic and Unhappy (2014) achieved – not least through sympathetic glimpses of his parents – an almost elegiac tone as he analysed Britain’s transition from a place of “job security, a semblance of social mobility, steadily rising living standards and a kind of permanence of things, of values and mores” to one where “the glue which bound us all together has dissolved” and “the furious yapping you hear” is the proclamation of outrage by competing grievance groups.

It was good that we have become more tolerant of diversity, he concluded, but “this sacking of the old order has left us fraught and clamorous, unhappy, isolated and averse.” One critic called the book “a flaming, bloodthirsty romp, scything through the lazy thinking of an effete liberal establishment”.

Similar descriptions were applied to his sell-out live performance, bottle of red wine to hand (in interview with the Spectator editor Fraser Nelson), at the 2,300-seat London Palladium in 2018: even a female Observer columnist, previously horrified by Liddle, had to admit he “sent me out of the theatre feeling quite a lot less gloomy”.

Nelson once observed that while “Don’t tone down Rod” was a plea he frequently heard from Spectator readers, Liddle was the writer most frequently deprecated by those who did not subscribe to the magazine. The bien-pensants of Twitter repeatedly fell for Liddle’s bait, tutting over articles such as the one in which he observed that he could never have worked as a teacher because he “could not remotely conceive of not trying to shag the kids”, although he observed in mitigation: “I don’t think I’d have dabbled much below year 10.”

What Liddle never did, in print or person, was hold himself up as anyone’s role model; indeed, it was sometimes evident that he despised himself almost as much as his targets. Acknowledging the mess of his personal life in middle age, he likened himself to the promiscuous North American montane vole. “In common parlance, I seemed to be the sort of chap who couldn’t keep it in his trousers.”

In 1993 he began a relationship with Rachel Royce, a television reporter whom he had met at the BBC. They had two sons, Tyler and Wilder, and were finally married in 2004, in a lavish holiday ceremony in Malaysia. But by then Liddle had begun an affair with The Spectator’s receptionist, Alicia Munckton, who was half his age and who broke off her engagement to another man; Rachel later claimed he left their honeymoon early to return to Alicia – while Liddle declared that “the failure was to have got married in the first place.”

He and Rachel proceeded to vent savage opinions of each other while the tabloids relished a new plot line in the unbuttoned soap opera that was The Spectator under the editorship of Boris Johnson. Liddle reported that Johnson “broke off discussing my next article to howl with laughter” at his discomfiture.

In 2005 Liddle was arrested and accepted a caution for common assault against Alicia during a domestic row when she was 20 weeks pregnant. When their daughter was born she was named Emmeline after the suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst.

Liddle was a member of the Labour Party for 40 years until he was expelled in 2016 for writing about “its strange affection for anti-Semitism”. In 2019 – the year he published The Great Betrayal, a study of the establishment’s attempts to thwart Brexit – he joined the Social Democratic Party; in the 2024 general election he stood as the SDP candidate in Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland, coming fourth.

Among his recent columns, devotees especially treasured an account of his (imagined) presence at the Bafta awards ceremony in which craven apologies were issued after an outburst by a Tourette’s campaigner: Liddle claimed to have bellowed “you self-important, preening, hideous, unnatural, waxen-skinned spaffgoblin” and “arse badger” at the compère without finding himself ejected by bouncers.

A surprising element of Liddle’s make-up, perhaps, was his Christian faith – expressed in a Christmas poem in The Spectator in 2017, in which he lamented the absence of Christ from a festival of “drivel on the telly, fake bonhomie, fake cheer” – but “somehow from up above, He watches… amused, appalled, distraught – who knows?”

Rod Liddle is survived by Alicia, whom he married in 2008, and his three children.

​Rod Liddle, born April 1 1960, died August 2 2026

data.title: France’s richest man has delivered a masterclass in playing the press
data.description:
Bernard Arnault is rich. Very rich. This, in broad brushstrokes, seems to be the finding of Le Monde’s six-part investigation into the chief executive of LVMH, which portrayed his business empire like a royal court – complete with guards, butlers, verbal beheadings and his children as rivalling heirs.

Hands up anyone out there with five kids who never bicker? Throw in a few reservoirs full of loose change and a hefty dose of power, and would you say that makes the odd tiff more or less likely? Either way, I’m guessing it was the focus on his children that tipped Arnault over the edge – and straight into a three-page open letter, published on X on July 26.

To say that this was uncharacteristic is an understatement. Ditching the loftiness and the discretion that have earned him nicknames like “the wolf in cashmere” – and had me in a cold sweat prior to my first of two interviews with Arnault, back in 2015 – the 77-year-old mocked the depiction of himself as head of “the last royal family of France”. He joked about Le Monde’s assertion that none of his staff was allowed to be overweight, insisted his children would henceforth be calling him “sir” and, crucially, ended the letter with good humour. “Rest assured, I will continue doing Le Monde’s crossword puzzles. Those, at least, are excellent.”

A week on, the letter has been viewed more than eight million times. It has been lauded in op-eds in the New York Times – “How to Change Your Image as a Heartless Luxury Titan Overnight” – and the Wall Street Journal – “Arnault is Changing The Playbook”. There’s no doubt that it was a masterclass in the art of the takedown – a document that should be studied by PRs and replicated in tone by public figures in need of “warming up” their image all over the world. But most importantly, it felt like the man I met.

Yes, it’s true that – as one of his closest friends, Pierre Godé, once said – Arnault “doesn’t smile at anything and everything”, but I’ve always liked people who make you earn a laugh. On both occasions when we sat down together, I glimpsed the humour beneath the famously impassive exterior.

Back in 2015, he told me about the surprise tennis game the children had laid on for him with Roger Federer. “Do you have any idea how much progress you make in just a few minutes playing opposite someone like Federer?” he quipped. And when I met up with him seven years later, I watched him laugh off his son’s gentle ribbing over technology, joke about meeting the “formidable” Queen and recount an amusing faux-pas with Elon Musk.

“You see, when he told me, ‘I’m going to colonise Mars’, I burst out laughing. Because I’ve never heard of such a thing, and I thought he was joking. But he was serious, and I don’t think he was best pleased,” he recalled.

If I were giving the “heartless luxury titans” of the world advice right now, I would keep it simple. When in doubt or under attack, make fun – preferably of yourself.

data.title: Burnham’s water nationalisation ‘risks costing taxpayers £140bn’
data.description:
Andy Burnham has been warned that nationalising Britain’s water sector would leave taxpayers facing a £140bn bill.

Creditors of Thames Water have told the Treasury that taxpayers would face an immediate compensation bill of up to £144bn to nationalise the water sector.

This is far higher than the official estimate of £100bn produced by regulator Ofwat, as it includes funding existing investment commitments as well as increases in inflation.

The estimate, which was produced by consultancy Frontier Economics on behalf of creditors of Thames Water, has been handed to the Government as the Prime Minister plots more state control of public utilities.

Uncertainty also hangs over the future of Thames Water, the UK’s biggest water supplier, which faces running out of money by November unless creditors inject more cash. A rescue deal was effectively blocked in June by Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary.

The report by Frontier Economics also warned that taxpayers would potentially be on the hook for hundreds of billions of pounds in extra costs over the coming decades if the water industry were to be nationalised. The sums would be needed to fund environmental obligations and infrastructure upgrades to support a rising population.

Ofwat’s official estimate of the cost of nationalising the water industry is based on the sector’s Regulatory Capital Value (RCV) – which forms the basis for how much water companies are allowed to charge customers.

Frontier Economics said its calculations were “driven primarily by the very substantial investment programmes” already agreed with the watchdog “that companies are undertaking and that private investors are financing”.

It also warned that bringing utilities under public control would probably take several years, pushing up the cost as inflation rises.

The consultancy also estimates that running costs for the sector in the next two decades could stretch into the hundreds of billions of pounds, which taxpayers would ultimately have to finance.

The report warned: “Costs falling to the public sector will not end at the point of nationalisation.

“In 2023, water companies estimated that meeting government targets and environmental obligations, in the context of climate change and population growth over the 20 years from 2030 to 2050, would cost £270bn.”

It added: “While these are sector costs, not nationalisation costs, under public ownership this investment would need to be financed by government spending or other forms of public debt before potentially being recouped through customer bills over the lives of these assets.”

Mr Burnham has made public control of utilities and other “essentials” a cornerstone of his premiership.

The former mayor of Manchester has said Thames Water should be nationalised, adding that public ownership of the water sector as a whole should “absolutely be an option”.

“I would say for Thames Water, that is what should be done,” he told The Guardian shortly before becoming Prime Minister.

Such a move would partially reverse Margaret Thatcher’s significant privatisation drive in the 1980s.

data.title: BP’s North Sea exit shows Miliband has been a disaster for Britain
data.description:
Ed Miliband leaves behind his role as Energy Secretary with the UK facing the highest industrial electricity costs in the world.

Industries such as chemicals and building materials are under enormous pressure.

And now as Foreign Secretary he is already swanning around the world, showboating on “moral leadership” instead of trying to rebuild relations with Donald Trump and support Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, in negotiating a better trade deal.

There are so many different ways that Miliband has damaged the British economy that it is often hard for even his most assiduous critics to keep track of them all. And yet there is one that should absolutely top the list.

With news that BP is exiting the North Sea, the destruction of a once-thriving oil and gas industry will go down as one of the greatest acts of economic self-sabotage of recent times – and Miliband is responsible.

It is impossible to blame BP for the decision to finally give up on the North Sea.

It was one of the pioneers of offshore oil exploration six decades ago, but it has now decided it is no longer worth the hassle.

A windfall tax confiscates any money it might make, it is subject to constant lawfare, and while Andy Burnham has signalled a more pragmatic approach, the Government has until now refused to give it permission to expand its fields.

While rivals such as Norway’s state-owned Equinor deliver bumper profits, driven by increased output in its share of the North Sea, BP faces nothing but restrictions and levies. It is only doing what makes sense for its shareholders, and that means retreating.

The trouble is, that is a disaster for the wider British economy.

We will have to wait to see who buys its assets off the coast of Aberdeen. But let’s not kid ourselves. It will probably be a private equity-backed asset-stripper intent on extracting as much cash as possible while the business is run down.

Whoever it is won’t have BP’s depth of expertise, nor its resources. The country will have taken another step towards closing down what should be one of our most valuable assets. And we need to be straightforward about the person responsible for that.

As energy secretary, Miliband made two crucial mistakes. First, he prioritised net zero over energy security.

Given that Britain accounts for less than 1pc of global emissions, and we have already dramatically reduced them (unfortunately almost entirely by closing down heavy manufacturing industries instead of switching to green production), there is relatively little that we can do about the state of the global climate, decarbonisation of the power grid aside.

But the security of our energy supplies is entirely within our own control, and anyone can see that domestic production is far more reliable, as well as better for the balance of payments, than oil and gas that has to be imported.

The energy secretary could have balanced the two, and reached a reasonable compromise, but Miliband gave no sign of even contemplating that.

Next, he failed to seize the opportunity to expand production, especially of gas, at a time when there was significant demand across Europe. It is not an issue of taking climate change seriously or not.

Everyone knows that we will need fossil fuels while making the transition to cleaner forms of energy, and they may as well create jobs and tax revenue in this country instead of in Qatar, the US or Norway.

If Miliband had demonstrated just a slither of flexibility, BP might still be expanding, instead of shutting down.

After his two years in power, Miliband has left a trail of damage in his wake. Energy prices have soared out of control.

Industrial energy is now four times more expensive in Britain than in the US, and twice the price of France, showing little sign of coming down any time soon.

That has made it completely impossible to remain competitive in industries such as steel or building materials where energy can account for 40pc to 50pc of the cost base.

And whole swathes of industry have been forced to close as the added costs of both energy and the green levies have crushed them.

Britain dropped out of the top 10 largest manufacturing nations last year, overtaken by rivals such as Taiwan, Mexico and even Russia, and shows little sign of recapturing that place now.

Meanwhile cement production has fallen to a 75-year low, meaning that even if the Government wanted to build houses, there wouldn’t be any domestic materials for the job.

Of course, there are different reasons for each decision. But Miliband’s disastrous decisions have clearly been a major factor.

It is going to become even worse. Instead of being thrown out of office, as any sensible prime minister would do, Burnham has promoted Miliband to Foreign Secretary.

Instead of going straight to Washington to try to lay the diplomatic groundwork to persuade the Trump administration to lift its latest round of tariffs on Britain, Miliband spent his first week in charge of foreign affairs flying to Spain for some meaningless waffle about fighting climate change together.

We can safely assume that backing the Business Secretary on the bread and butter issues of tariffs, trade deals and promoting exports, which should be the core priorities for the Foreign Secretary of a country with massive debts and desperately in need of a boost to growth, will be forgotten about for the next few years, while they will have plenty of photo ops where Miliband can boast about “moral leadership”.

Red Ed has turned into a one-man wrecking ball, taking out huge chunks of our industrial base, destroying the North Sea,and patting himself on the back as the country’s energy supply becomes more precarious.

BP’s exit from the North Sea is just the latest, and perhaps the most dramatic example, of his unique talent for destruction. Unfortunately there is little sign that he is finished yet.
