data.title: Where to put £100k savings right now for the highest return
data.description:
Have you got a savings strategy to maximise your returns? We want to hear from you. Email money@telegraph.co.uk

The great savings rate decline may not happen this year, as conflict in Iran has halted plans for further Bank Rate reductions. While this is good news for your savings, it’s tempered by the fact that inflation is expected to rise, eating away at your returns.

To protect your money, it’s worth putting some effort into finding the accounts paying the best rates possible.

But with so many to choose from, all with differing rates and conditions, finding the best home for your cash can be difficult. Everyone’s circumstances are different: some can afford to lock cash away for years, while others only feel comfortable if they can make instant withdrawals in case of emergencies.

Telegraph Money asked Katie Horne of Flagstone, a cash deposit platform, to give her views on three scenarios that represent common questions we get asked by readers.

For simplicity’s sake, we have not considered tax. In reality, tax on savings interest would be a problem for any money held outside an Isa.

Once you earn interest over £1,000 a year (for most basic-rate taxpayers) or £500 (for higher-rate payers), returns are subject to income tax, due to the personal savings allowance.

Scenario 1

A retired couple in their 70s with £100,000 in cash. They are happy to lock up £80,000 for more than a year, but need access to the rest – though not necessarily daily

Katie says: “The retired couple could take advantage of some longer-term fixed accounts, specifically the Punjab National Bank 12-month Fixed Term Deposit, which pays 4.72pc.

“They can place £80,000 into this product, earning themselves interest of £3,776 a year. If they are comfortable securing a longer fixed term, and concerned that rates might be significantly lower in 12 months’ time, another option is Chetwood Bank’s 5 Year Fixed Term Deposit, paying 5.04pc AER, which would generate £3,672 a year in interest.

“For the remaining £20,000, they could use their Isa allowance – Aldermore Bank Instant Access Cash Isa pays 3.77pc AER, generating interest of £754 a year.

“However, if they have used their Isa allowance, they could choose the Shawbrook Bank instant access account, paying 3.98pc AER, earning £796 in interest.

“All of these accounts would be covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS). This balanced portfolio would meet their near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.42pc to 4.57pc, equivalent to between £4,426 and £4,572 a year.”

Scenario 2

A working woman in her 50s with £100,000 in cash. She needs ready access to £80,000 but can lock up £20,000 for up to three years

Katie says: “She could opt to place £80,000 into an instant-access account from Shawbrook Bank, which pays 3.98pc AER.

“This account allows unlimited withdrawals without any restrictions and would earn her £3,184 in interest a year.

“If she is willing to restrict access somewhat, she could achieve a slightly higher rate with Gatehouse Bank’s three-month fixed term product, currently paying 4.16pc AER, earning £3,280 in interest a year.

“For the remaining £20,000, she could secure the ICICI Bank 5 Year Fixed Term Deposit, currently paying 4.59pc, earning £918 a year in interest. Alternatively, she could lock in for a shorter period and secure a slightly higher rate of 4.72pc with the Punjab National Bank 12 Month Fixed Term Deposit, earning £944 a year.

“Her selection here would probably be driven by her view on the likelihood of significantly lower savings rates in 12-18 months.

“This balanced portfolio would meet her near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.1pc to 4.31pc, or £4,102 to £4,312, again covered by the FSCS.”

Scenario 3

A working man in his 40s. Has no savings, but can put aside £1,500 a month for the next five years. Doesn’t need access for five years

Katie says: “A number of big banks offer good savings rates with specific requirements. For example, Santander Edge Saver offers 6pc AER with a minimum deposit of £1 and a maximum deposit of £4,000, or £233 a year in interest. Once his savings have grown, he can reassess and diversify his investments.

“We would also suggest that he look into cash Isas to take advantage of the tax-free status. You can currently invest up to £20,000 in Isas each year without paying tax on the interest you earn.

“The best rates over the past 12 months have been around the 4.5pc mark. Currently, Trading 212 offers a cash Isa at 4.51pc with no minimum required. If he puts in £300 a month, he’ll get a return of £80 a year.”

Scenario 4

A saver in their 60s with £100,000 in cash. They don’t need access to all of this money immediately, but want to generate a steady return while keeping some flexibility

Katie says: “For savers who want to strike a balance between flexibility and income, laddering fixed-term deposits can be a really effective strategy. It allows you to earn higher returns on money you don’t need straight away, while keeping some accessible in case of emergencies.

“In this example, £25,000 could be held in an easy access account with Shawbrook Bank, paying 3.98pc AER, earning £995 in annual interest.

“A further £25,000 could be placed in a six-month fixed term account from Progressive Building Society, paying 4.35pc AER, earning £1,088 in interest over the year.

“For the next portion, £25,000 could be locked into a 12-month fixed term deposit from Punjab National Bank, paying 4.72pc, which would generate £1,180 in annual interest.

“The final £25,000 could go into a 24-month fixed term deposit from ICICI Bank, paying 4.46pc AER, earning £1,115 a year.

“This combination would provide access to a portion of funds at all times, while maintaining steady income from staggered maturities. It also ensures full FSCS protection across four banks, a key advantage of spreading deposits.

“Altogether, this portfolio would achieve an average blended rate of 4.38pc, generating around £4,378 in annual interest, with funds maturing every six to 12 months to allow reinvestment at new market rates.”

data.title: Currys’ turnaround king tasked with reviving tired Boots ahead of flotation
data.description:
When Currys announced that Alex Baldock, its chief executive, was stepping down earlier this year, the response from investors was immediate.

Shares in the electronics chain fell sharply – wiping almost 11pc off its valuation – as markets digested the departure of the man widely credited with engineering the company’s quietly successful turnaround.

Now Baldock appears poised for an even bigger challenge, tasked with reviving a 177-year-old brand that has seen better days. On Wednesday, it emerged that the outgoing Currys chief was being lined up to take the reins at Boots.

The company confirmed his appointment on Thursday, setting the stage for Baldock to try to convince investors that the British chemist could be worth as much as £7bn.

Baldock should be well-suited to the role. He has spent the past seven years proving that legacy retailers can still thrive if they modernise quickly enough.

At Currys, that meant slimming down the store estate, cutting costs, boosting online sales and emphasising its “omnichannel” offering of services, repairs, credit and subscriptions.

Adam Tomlinson, a retail analyst at Berenberg, says that when Baldock arrived at Currys in 2018, “the business was in a very tough place”.

“A major focus initially was restructuring the mobile division, which had become a significant drag on the wider group. He completely realigned it in terms of right-sizing both the store base and the cost base, and turned it from being a problem area into a positive contributor.”

Tomlinson says Baldock’s broader strategy has been to transform Currys from a “product-first retailer into an integrated services business”, encouraging customer loyalty through credit offers, delivery and installation, warranties, repairs and trade-ins.

“What is often overlooked is how much focus he placed on staff and colleagues,” he adds. “He has a mantra that customer experience can never exceed colleague experience.”

Baldock will now have to repeat that success at Boots – a brand which is desperately in need of a turnaround.

Since being folded into Walgreens Boots Alliance in 2014, Boots has endured closures, restructurings and repeated attempts to move away from its old-fashioned chemist image.

Its owners have repeatedly signalled that they would be keen to offload the British business. Walgreens launched a sale process for Boots in 2022.

However, it later scrapped the plans after failing to secure a deal at the valuation it wanted in the face of difficult market conditions and rising borrowing costs. Since then, efforts have been focused on honing the chain, including pushing through further store closures and cost reductions.

Speculation over a sell-off of the British arm was revived last year when private equity firm Sycamore Partners swooped to buy Walgreens Boots Alliance in a $10bn (£7.4bn) deal.

Shortly after the deal was completed, Sycamore split Walgreens into five standalone entities – one of which was Boots. It was seen as the first major step towards ultimately returning the British chemist to the UK stock market.

Baldock is believed by many to have been brought on to get Boots over the line for such a London listing – something insiders claim was “always the plan”. Its owners are looking for a valuation as high as £7bn. Still, some remain unconvinced that any listing would be imminent.

A senior retail industry source says his appointment is the same “as with any private equity-owned business”. “The job is to create as much value as possible for the owners,” the source says.

Given the current state of the London market, they say it is more likely that Baldock has simply been brought in to put Boots on a stronger footing. “I don’t think it’s right that he’s been brought in for an IPO.”

They say Boots’ health and beauty division is now “by far the most important part of the business”, reflecting the growing view inside retail that the future of Boots lies less in pharmacy and more in cosmetics, skincare and wellness.

That shift is already visible inside many of Boots’ larger stores, where beauty halls increasingly dominate the shop floor while traditional pharmacy space shrinks.

Boots has revamped more than 100 of its stores and updated beauty halls in more than 180 sites. It argues that this has helped it to record 20 consecutive quarters of market-share growth.

Analysts expect Baldock to continue pushing the business in the same direction because beauty products offer significantly stronger margins than dispensing medicines or selling low-cost healthcare essentials.

Jonathan De Mello, of JDM Retail, says Boots is “looking at devoting more floor space to beauty rather than distress pharmaceutical purchasing. The margins on beauty products are significantly better”.

At the same time, Boots still faces the challenge of balancing investment in physical stores with the need to boost online sales.

For all the investment Boots has poured into flagship stores and digital infrastructure, analysts argue the business still lags behind rivals on both fronts.

“The Advantage Card is strong, but the website still needs work,” says De Mello.

Former executives claim there are also still swathes of its sprawling estate which are in urgent need of investment. Renovating all of these old stores would be painfully expensive.

Clive Black, another retail analyst, agrees the chain’s estate remains uneven despite years of investment.

“There are some flagship stores where they have clearly invested heavily in beauty, but there are also an awful lot of stores around the country that look pretty tired,” says Black.

If Baldock wants to take Boots public – be it later this year or further down the line – he will have to convince investors that Boots can be a growth business rather than simply a reliable cash generator.

Black says he suspects that “Boots may end up being seen more as an income story than a pure growth story”.

Baldock will also inherit questions over Boots’ international operations.

While the retailer’s presence outside the UK may have formed part of the attraction for him personally – having steered Currys for years in both the UK and overseas – analysts suggest some international businesses could ultimately be sold off as management focuses more tightly on the chain’s strongest markets.

De Mello says Boots’ operations in places such as Germany and Mexico are underperforming. He argues the business would be better concentrating on the UK and Ireland, which he describes as the company’s “engine room for growth”.

At Currys, Baldock managed to convince the markets that physical stores still had value in the Amazon era, provided they worked seamlessly alongside a strong online offer. Between 2024 and 2026, he oversaw a tripling in the retailer’s share price.

Just last week, Baldock told The Times that he loved his role at Currys. His next move would have to be “something properly exciting to take me away from Currys”. With Boots, it seems that Baldock has found that. Now, he said, marked the start of “an exciting new chapter for Boots”.

data.title: Britain’s biggest power plant demands damages over grid delays
data.description:
Britain’s state-owned grid operator should be made liable for damages over delayed upgrades to the country’s electricity network, the owner of the UK’s biggest power station has said.

Will Gardiner, the chief executive of Drax, said the National Energy System Operator (Neso) and the other companies behind Britain’s power networks should be made liable for failures that hold up vital new connections needed to keep the lights on.

The UK’s power grid has been under strain this summer as heatwaves forced Neso to scramble to import more electricity supplies in June.

The grid operator has also been grappling with a significant backlog of power projects – including many speculative or unviable schemes – that have been asking to connect to the UK’s electricity networks.

Mr Gardiner called on Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, to change the law to allow power plant developers “to get paid damages when connections are not made on a date for which there is contractual certainty”.

“It needs a significant fundamental system change,” he said. “Because right now, the system operator and the transmission and distribution companies have no liability for missing the connection dates that they’re giving us.”

Mr Gardiner said Drax, which operates a four-gigawatt plant in Yorkshire, had been promised connection dates for a series of new gas facilities but these timelines had been repeatedly pushed back.

Mr Gardiner said Drax had completed three gas-fired power plants three years ago but only one has been connected to the wider UK network so far, leaving the other two sitting idle even as extreme temperatures left Neso racing to secure extra electricity on June 23.

The Drax boss said these projects could have helped Britain weather a power supply crunch that threatened the UK’s “system security”.

“We were originally told that the new gas power stations would be connected in 2024,” Mr Gardiner said. “Now it’s 2026 and one of them is connected but the other two are not.

“They send letters offering a connection date and then six months later, they send another letter with a later date. There’s no contractual certainty in either one of those letters and so there is no recourse for the costs we incur.”

Neso has been attempting to reform the UK’s queuing system for linking new power plants to the grid. This previously worked on a first-come, first-served basis but subsidies on offer to renewable generators saw dozens of new and untested operators demand connections for wind and solar farms.

By 2024, there were enough proposals to supply the UK eight times over, creating a bottleneck that is taking years to resolve.

Drax operates Britain’s most controversial power station, the wood-burning Drax plant in Yorkshire, which burns six million to seven million trees and emits 12 million tonnes of CO2 a year.

Its power is deemed green by Neso, which classifies forests as a “renewable” resource.

The company has been diversifying into new forms of generation including wind, solar and battery storage, as well as building three new gas power stations that can be switched on when wind output is low.

Neso has said its offers of connection dates depend on whether upgrades to the wider UK power grid are completed on time by transmission operators.

“Connections reform is designed to prioritise projects that are ready to progress and strategically needed for Great Britain’s future energy needs,” Neso said.

A spokesman for the Energy Networks Association, which represents the UK’s operators including National Grid and UK Power Networks, said: “Neso and the networks are continuing to issue offers to transmission and distribution projects under the agreed joint industry plan.”

data.title: North Sea is not competitive, BP boss says
data.description:
The boss of BP has declared the North Sea is not competitive as pressure grows on Andy Burnham to scrap the oil and gas windfall tax.

Meg O’Neill, who took over as chief executive in April, said she had spoken with the Prime Minister and urged him to make it more attractive to exploit Britain’s domestic energy resources.

However, Ms O’Neill said BP would not change its mind about its decision to sell its North Sea assets.

The company put its UK operations up for sale last week, potentially ending the oil giant’s six decades of production in the basin.

Ms O’Neill told CNBC on Tuesday: “When we look at how it fits into our portfolio today, it just doesn’t compete for capital.”

Speaking to journalists, she said: “We do still see growth potential in the North Sea – there’s still undeveloped fields there. We would love to see exploration resume in the North Sea.

“But from an investment perspective, dollars spent in the North Sea are just not as competitive as other opportunities.”

Ms O’Neill said constant changes to the taxation of oil and gas in during the past 20 years had undermined the company’s faith in investing in the British North Sea.

Ms O’Neill said she was talking to the Government about “designing a fiscal framework” that would encourage oil and gas extraction, but warned that any changes were “not going to change our mind” about exiting the North Sea.

The move has raised fears that BP could quit Britain by moving its stock market listing to the US or shifting its headquarters.

Ms O’Neill said BP had no plans to leave the London Stock Exchange, where it is a keystone company in the FTSE 100 Index.

BP more than doubled its profits in the first half of the year as the Iran war boosted oil trading and its refining margins.

Its underlying replacement cost profit surged by 139pc to $8.9bn (£6.6bn) in the first six months of 2026.

However, it also revealed that Labour’s extension of the windfall tax raid on North Sea profits had added $539m to its tax bill last year and another $97m so far this year.

BP’s decision to quit the North Sea comes after Labour increased the tax, called the energy profits levy, when it came to power. This took the headline tax rate on North Sea profits to 78pc. Labour also extended the tax by two years from 2028 to 2030.

According to BP’s tax report for 2025, the energy giant generated £3.4bn for the Treasury last year.

This contribution will fall sharply as soon as BP completes the sale of its North Sea assets.

BP has five oil platforms in the North Sea employing around 1,100 people. The company remains headquartered in the UK and Ms O’Neill said last week that Britain “will continue to play an important role in our future”.

‘Use domestic resources first’

Ms O’Neill said the company had received several unsolicited approaches for its assets in the basin, which she said could be “profitable in the hands of a future owner”.

She told CNBC: “I’ve had a conversation with the Prime Minister where he reinforced his desire to work closely with business, to be pragmatic.

“The message I left him with was: the UK gets 75pc of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas.

“The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.”

She added: “We ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party.”

Labour has been accused of dithering over the granting of licences to drill in the North Sea.

Ed Miliband failed to give the go-ahead for extraction to begin at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the basin while he was energy secretary under Sir Keir Starmer. Miatta Fahnbulleh, his successor, is expected to approve new drilling.

BP came close to selling its North Sea operations to energy business Ithaca Energy earlier this year in a deal that would have valued the division at about £2bn. However, the talks fell apart.

The Scottish Government has also ramped up pressure on Labour to scrap the oil and gas windfall tax.

John Swinney, the First Minister, said: “It is crystal clear that the UK Government’s destructive tax regime is harming investment and jobs in Scotland – and the new Prime Minister must look at this issue as a matter of urgency.”

Donald Trump added to calls for the UK to reopen the North Sea, with the US president warning on Monday that Britain risked becoming a “bankrupt country”.

He said: “If you open up, you’d be a wealthy country. You keep it closed, you’re going to be a bankrupt country.”

Mr Burnham said he was “looking at” the windfall tax.

BP’s results also revealed it had continued its “green retreat”, announcing the sale of Archaea Energy, its US renewable natural gas business acquired in 2022 for $4.1bn.

The purchase was part of its push to expand aggressively in renewables, a strategy BP abandoned in 2025 to refocus on oil and gas. It ⁠has written off billions from its low-carbon businesses so far this year.

data.title: Shops hit with higher taxes for installing air-con
data.description:
High-street shops face paying more tax if they install air conditioning to keep customers cool in the summer, retail bosses have warned.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said businesses were being punished for spending money on cooling units to lower indoor temperatures as stores struggled with repeated heatwaves this year.

She said: “Climate change continues to deliver more and more extreme temperatures in the UK. 

“Retailers are responding by investing in both mitigations – such as more air conditioning and more efficient refrigeration units – and in sustainability initiatives aimed at reducing carbon emissions.”

Ms Dickinson added: “Unfortunately, business rates often punish stores for such investments, showing the need for Government to look again at this broken system.”

Interest in air conditioning has been growing this year amid sustained high temperatures.

However, the technology has proved to be controversial as its use drives up energy consumption at a time when bills are already high and the grid is under strain.

Tom Ironside, the director of business and regulation at the BRC, said the problem with air conditioning is that the tax is levied based on the value of a property, which is increased by the investment.

He said: “Adding improvements, such as air conditioning, to a property leads to an increase in its rateable value and, as a result, its business rates liability. This effectively penalises stores for making this investment.

“So long as this is the case, retailers will either have to be prepared to shoulder higher costs when they install air conditioning systems or put off much-needed investment in measures to modernise stores.”

Shops can secure a reprieve on higher tax bills if they install air-con through so-called “improvement relief”, but this only lasts for one year before the rates rise again.

Business rates are set to raise £37bn for the Government this financial year, up from £34bn last year and £32bn in 2024-25.

The revenue from the tax has increased because of factors including revaluations, rising multipliers for high-value premises and the withdrawal of Covid-era reliefs for the retail and hospitality sectors.

The number of shoppers visiting stores fell by 2.1pc in July compared with the same month of a year ago, according to the BRC. High streets are suffering more than other retail destinations, with visitor numbers down 3.8pc.

Footfall has been down in six of the seven months of this year so far, with rain at the start of 2026 and repeated heatwaves blamed.

English retailers are feeling the worst effects, with footfall up in Scotland, which has tended to experience cooler temperatures than the South.

A Treasury spokesman said: “Supporting businesses to invest, grow and deal with cost pressures is a key priority for the Chancellor. 

“Businesses can receive relief on their business rates bills through improvement relief when they upgrade their properties with certain improvements, including installing air conditioning.”

data.title: Britain cannot afford to gamble on a bank tax raid
data.description:
For a man who promised to usher in a new era of hope and change, Andy Burnham’s Government is already sounding and behaving an awful lot like the old one.

Perhaps that’s not surprising given that many of the faces around the Cabinet table had been there before under Sir Keir Starmer. Maybe Burnham thought by giving them new jobs nobody would notice.

Still, that’s no excuse for the sort of rehashed drivel that John Healey served up at the weekend with a warning to supermarkets that the Treasury would crack down on any “price-gouging” at either “the pump or the till”.

These are the same worn-out clichés that Rachel Reeves turned to whenever she needed a convenient scapegoat for the cost of living crisis.

Having disingenuously pointed the finger at the supermarkets and petrol forecourts as a primary cause of voters’ hardship, the fear among bank bosses is that they’re next in the firing line.

With good reason too, given the Government’s refusal on Thursday to rule out higher bank taxes in the upcoming Budget.

While Burnham may see any attempt to impose higher levies on the industry as a sure-fire vote-winner, a bank tax raid is a populist gamble that broke Britain cannot afford to take.

The temptation is obvious: like the oil giants – another favourite punch bag of the Left – the banks are once again raking it in on the back of a major global crisis that has made it even harder for millions of households to make ends meet.

Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – racked up almost £30bn in profits in the first half of the year, much of it the result of higher interest rates ushered in within days of Donald Trump waging war on Iran.

It could have stopped there, of course, but this is an industry that has never been good at reading the room and in many ways is its own worst enemy.

At a time when Burnham was looking for evidence of “profiteering”, the banks thought it would be a great moment to lavish bumper pay rises on their already handsomely paid executives and hand billions of pounds back to shareholders in the City.

Almost half the profits amassed by the Big Four – £13.7bn – will be returned to investors in the form of dividends and share buybacks. This is a red rag to a bull.

So when campaigners seize on this as further evidence of the need for a windfall tax, the industry can hardly sit there and claim it is being unfairly targeted.

Yet, that doesn’t necessarily mean higher bank levies would be a smart move. On the contrary, it would almost certainly be a recklessly harmful one.

I’m not sure I believe those bank bosses who warn further tax raids would be the trigger for some sort of wholesale exodus of foreign banks.

There have been no end of similar warnings every time the bank levy issue rears its ugly head, none of which have ever come to fruition.

But I do think there is the risk that planned investment in the UK is quickly redirected elsewhere, or worse, that higher taxes quickly result in cut-backs to help fund any fresh tax raid.

For years, politicians ignored industry warnings about the effect of a windfall tax on the oil and gas industry – introduced by the Tories, it is worth remembering – but Westminster largely dismissed them.

The results of that astonishing arrogance are now painfully plain to see. 

In the face of one of the most punitive tax regimes in the world, numerous firms have scaled down capital spending in the North Sea or turned their attention to other parts of the world. 

Others have announced plans to wind down their operations in the region, while some have chosen to exit altogether.

BP’s decision to pull out of Britain’s coastal waters after 60 years is the death knell for a corner of the economy that employs thousands and remains a pillar – albeit a rapidly dwindling one – of energy security and independence.

To wilfully oversee its destruction is an act of profound self-harm. In the face of disruption to Middle East energy supplies, the smart strategy would be to ensure that those who haven’t yet given up on the North Sea stay and invest.

Instead, the sector faces accusations from the Green Party that it is “cashing in on human misery”, alongside preposterous demands for them to be hit with higher taxes still to pay for firefighting helicopters. 

Zack Polanski even suggested fossil fuel firms should not be making “a single penny of profit”.

For such opponents it hardly matters that the oil and gas industry is already a significant source of tax revenue. BP’s tax bill for 2025 alone was £1.2bn.

The banking industry meanwhile was responsible for more than £43bn of taxes last year – equivalent to nearly 5pc of the total UK tax take.

Yet the likes of Polanski and the Trade Union Congress are so ideologically inclined to blame big business for the country’s chief ills that they refuse to consider the unintended consequences of their endless quest to lump yet more tax on these industries.

It’s not just that Labour’s perpetual tax squeeze on business puts the brakes on growth, these policies pose a real danger of causing serious and irreparable damage to the economy.

Companies will vote with their feet, and in the case of the North Sea that is exactly what is happening. 

The next shoe to drop is BP or Shell shifting share listings and headquarters overseas and turning their backs on the UK altogether if hostility deepens, potentially taking billions of taxes with them.

A decade ago, HSBC triggered a political storm when it threatened to abandon the UK in response to a manifesto commitment from the then-Labour Opposition to raise the bank levy by a further £800m a year.

Stuart Gulliver, the chairman of HSBC at the time, said he was facing “significant pressure from shareholders” to relocate to Hong Kong.

Some thought it was little more than an empty threat. Either way, it was successful in persuading George Osborne, then Chancellor, to scale back the scope of the existing bank levy so that it only applied to UK-based balance sheets, rather than global assets.

So when Dame Jane Fraser, the Scottish-born chief executive of Citigroup investment bank, warns that a fresh tax raid on banks would hurt Britain, Burnham and Healy have little choice but to assume she’s being serious.

Ditto when Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, says there would be “adverse consequences” if Mr Burnham targeted lenders with higher taxes.

With the nation’s finances in a far more precarious state today, Burnham and Healey are simply in no position to call their bluff.

There is growing evidence the UK is experiencing meaningful capital flight at both the individual and corporate level as a result of Labour’s ruinous tax policies. 

This must be reversed, not accelerated if Britain is to avoid sinking into the financial abyss.

data.title: Net zero tycoons lash out at Britain’s power grid
data.description:
Two net zero tycoons have criticised the National Energy System Operator (Neso) after being told their projects must wait more than a decade to be connected to the grid.

Chris Marsh, the chief executive of solar developer Enviromena, and Ben Guest, who runs grid battery specialist Gresham House Energy Storage, have been warned by Neso their projects would take up to 13 years to secure a connection.

Each has poured tens of millions of pounds into low-carbon developments based on promises of a rapid grid hook-up.

But a logjam of connection applications to Neso has stalled approvals, with Guest saying many of his battery storage projects were being given dates in the late 2030s.

He says: “Connection dates into the late 2030s are a reality of the current system ... offers now range from the late 2020s through to 2035, and in a meaningful number of cases, beyond that. And it isn’t one or two projects – it’s across the industry.”

His warnings were backed by Marsh, who has two dozen solar plants and plans for another gigawatts-worth – much of which he can’t build.

“We are being offered connections in 2038 ... The frustration is everywhere,” he adds.

Their warnings follow a similar attack by Will Gardiner, the chief executive of the Drax Group, whose three new gas-fired power stations have waited three years for a grid connection.

Two were left idle even as June’s extreme temperatures left Neso begging France for power to keep the UK’s lights on.

Neso has been under fire in recent weeks because of claims that its staff were involved in a cover-up of blackout risks.

The organisation has hired an independent law firm to investigate the allegations, after Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, claimed staff were told not to leave a paper trail about attempts to stabilise the grid during June’s heatwave.

But the approval logjam raises questions about how Britain could end up with such a long delay in connecting renewable projects – especially when the UK has been begging developers to build more low-carbon infrastructure.

Guest says the problem of connection delays went back years as successive governments offered ever greater subsidies to developers building new renewables.

The aim was good, but, he says, the organisation was terrible.

It meant developers drew up plans for thousands of new renewable projects and swamped the system with connection requests.

‘Connection delays of over a decade’

But none of the 11 energy secretaries who have held office since 2010 worked out an organised way to assess and connect all those low-carbon projects.

Their legacy is a logjam that has paralysed the system for connecting new assets – and which could now scupper Britain’s plans for clean power by 2030 – or even 2035.

Guest says: “The queue became hugely oversubscribed, with more than 700 gigawatt (GW) of projects waiting for connections, but the country only needs a fraction of that to meet its clean power targets.

“Neso’s response was to pause acceptances and review every single connection offer in the queue to see if it was genuine or speculation. The time that has taken means we now have connection delays of over a decade.”

For companies such as Gresham, which are funding and building the UK’s future power networks, the crisis goes beyond just delays and deep into its finances.

But it is also set to hit energy bills. The value of batteries lies in their ability to soak up power when it’s plentiful, such as on windy days, and then release it when the wind slumps or demand soars.

It means batteries can buffer the peaks and troughs of power generation in a system increasingly dominated by renewables – keeping overall prices down.

Their deployment is estimated to have saved £188m on power bills in the last 18 months and, unlike solar and wind, they need no subsidies.

Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, wanted Britain’s battery power to increase from its current 7GW capacity to 35GW by 2050 – a five-fold increase.

But with Neso in charge, warns Guest, that’s just wishful thinking.

For solar developers such as Enviromena, the dynamics are different but the problem is the same.

Labour wants solar capacity to increase from 20GW now to more than 100GW by 2050, but its own connection system is stopping that happening.

Marsh has spent tens of millions gaining the land and planning permission to double the 300 megawatts (MW) he already has, but he faces years of waiting to recoup his costs.

“We have an additional 300MW that is fully consented and ready to build, but we don’t have the grid connections for at least five years, and that’s holding up roughly £150m,” he says.

Perhaps ironically one of the Enviromena projects being held up by both planning and connection issues lies in Doncaster North, the constituency of Miliband – who oversaw the creation of Neso in 2024.

“We have even emailed Fintan Slye, the chief executive of Neso, but we don’t get any response – they aren’t listening to us. And there are millions of pounds at stake. Just getting a project to the point where we can seek a connection costs £500,000,” Marsh adds.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, now overseen by Miatta Fahnbulleh, says its reforms will save money but admits to the delays. “We are actively working with Neso Ofgem and network companies to prevent any further delays.”

Neso said the system it inherited when it was set up in 2025 was “unfit for purpose” and took time to unravel. “We are prioritising projects that are ready to progress and strategically needed for Great Britain’s future energy needs.”

But for generators, however, the key question is how Fahnbulleh’s predecessors as energy secretary allowed such a chaotic situation to develop in the first place.

Entrepreneurs such as Guest and Marsh point out that energy projects take years of planning and include complex engineering and financing – so they can only succeed if politicians are consistent in policy.

However, in the 14 years of the Conservative and coalition governments the energy secretary post changed hands 10 times. Andrea Leadsom was in post for just six months and Jacob Rees-Mogg for just a few weeks.

Opponents trace much of the current connection chaos directly back to the swings in policy-making and implementation that went with such inconstancy.

Under Labour, in power for just two years, there have already been two more energy secretaries.

Regulator Ofgem has been overseeing the UK’s energy networks for the last 25 years, and so is widely regarded as another of the architects of the current chaos.

But it is now also in the strange position of threatening others with fines if they fail to put it right.

A spokesman said: “We have introduced tough new incentives to hold network companies to account, including financial penalties where they fail to deliver timely connections.”

Few in the trade believe that will be enough.

Solar Energy UK, RenewableUK and Scottish Renewables wrote to regulator Ofgem in June about the “increasingly critical issue surrounding grid connection offers and the severe implications this is having for renewable energy development across the UK.”

But for Marsh, the buck stops with Neso.

“Neso holds all the strings, but they aren’t talking to us,” he says.

data.title: Solar eclipse to force Britain to fire up gas power stations
data.description:
An eclipse of the sun will force Britain to fire up its gas power stations as solar energy plummets.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), which manages Britain’s electricity grid, expects gas-fired plants to step up production as solar output falls by up to 1.3 gigawatts (GW). This is similar to losing the output of two of the UK’s operating nuclear reactors.

The solar eclipse, which will occur on Wednesday Aug 12, will be the largest visible in the UK since 1999.

A Neso analyst said: “The effects of the eclipse are quite far-reaching geographically, all the way across Europe, and to America as well.

“There’s a peak obscuration of about 95pc, so 95pc of the sun will be blocked by the Moon.

“This will have an effect on the solar generation ... and as a prudent network operator, we have been analysing this since about one year ago, looking at the expected size of the effect on the embedded generation.”

Swings in power output can destabilise the grid if not controlled, but Neso expects the predicted drop to be well within manageable limits using back-up gas and battery systems.

The eclipse will take place from 6pm to 8pm, meaning the lost solar output will be smaller than if it were to happen at midday.

However, generators have been told to be ready with extra capacity.

During the event, the Moon’s shadow will move from north to south, with the strongest effect on western Britain and the weakest in the east. It means solar plants in Wales, Devon and Cornwall will experience the biggest decrease in output.

The Neso analyst said the decline in output was most likely to be around 0.7GW, but could be as much as 1.3GW depending on how sunny the preceding hours had been.

Solar power can add a maximum of about 16GW to the UK’s generating capacity on a sunny day.

Neso’s concern follows the heavy scrutiny it has faced in recent weeks because of unrelated claims that its staff were involved in a cover-up of power outage risks.

The organisation has hired an independent law firm to investigate the allegations, after Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, claimed staff were told not to leave a paper trail about attempts to stabilise the grid during June’s heatwave.

More recently it has been criticised by senior figures in the renewables industry because of the chaos surrounding its management of the queue for new connections.

A Neso spokesman said the predicted fall in solar output was well within the system’s ability to cope.

The spokesman said: “The eclipse is a predictable event that has been factored into operational planning well in advance.

“A temporary reduction in solar output is expected during the eclipse, but Great Britain’s electricity system is designed to accommodate changes in generation throughout the day.

“Market participants are able to plan for these changes ahead of time, and Neso will continue to use its normal operational processes to ensure electricity supply and demand remain in balance.”

data.title: Takeover saga pushes The Telegraph to a loss
data.description:
The Telegraph slipped to a loss of nearly £4m last year despite its strong underlying profits, as the paralysis and costs of its three-year ownership battle took a toll.

Newly filed 2025 accounts for Telegraph Media Group Holdings show a loss before tax of £3.9m on a turnover of £273.2m.

Revenues fell marginally from £279.4m in 2024 under pressure from declining sales of print newspapers to subscribers and in shops, and of print advertising. Print accounted for 53pc of turnover.

Meanwhile, digital subscriptions and advertising revenue both grew by 8pc. At the end of the year there were 947,000 digital subscribers across all products, including a Puzzles app.

The ongoing rise of AI answers, which crimps traffic from Google search, hit turnover from Telegraph Travel and other lifestyle journalism by 20pc.

Yet the balanced performance in highly restrictive circumstances meant The Telegraph continued to deliver the strong underlying profits that helped draw a knockout bid from its new owner, the global publisher Axel Springer.

Excluding exceptional costs, at the Telegraph’s parent company Press Acquisitions Limited, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation were £50.5m, down from £61.2m in 2024. At this level, pre-tax profit increased from £7.6m to £13.8m.

Axel Springer and Mathias Döpfner, its chairman, have pledged to invest in the digital growth of The Telegraph. A new chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol, will soon begin work with a remit to accelerate digital change that has been held back and deliver international and UK expansion.

Patrick Wehrmann, the new chief financial officer, said the business had been “resilient” and had significant opportunities ahead in events and the United States.

The new era has arrived not a moment too soon. On a statutory pre-tax basis, Telegraph Media Group Holdings was driven into the red by a combination of cash handed to advisers and non-cash reductions in the value of intangible assets.

Three years of accounts for The Telegraph’s parent company show that the total paid to lawyers, accountants, bankers and various consultants has now exceeded £40m. Axel Springer completed its takeover at the end of June and further fees are expected for the current year.

The non-cash costs were prompted mostly by a restructuring which transferred the Telegraph operating business into a new shell company and severed risky links with its former owners, the Barclay family.

There was also an impairment of £4.2m on the valuation of the Chelsea Magazine Company, a niche lifestyle publisher acquired by Nick Hugh, the former chief executive, for £13m in 2023, shortly before The Telegraph was cast into limbo by the financial delinquency of the Barclays.

Their borrowing triggered a three-year crisis in June 2023, when Lloyds Banking Group seized The Telegraph via receivers. The lender was seeking to recover £1.2bn in overdue debt on which The Telegraph had been pledged as security.

Lloyds recovered the debt in full when the Barclay family made a complex deal intended to deliver ownership to the United Arab Emirates. Instead it prompted changes in the law to prevent foreign state ownership of UK news outlets and imposed massive costs and uncertainty, which were only ended by Axel Springer’s decisive £575m bid in March.

The new accounts suggest that the strains of the process were beginning to tell. They reveal that a “third party” – understood to be Axel Springer – stepped in with a £7m loan when cash appeared to be tight and normal corporate financing avenues were closed off by the ownership uncertainty.

The Telegraph continued to trade well and generate significant cash, but a £50m corporate debt with Lloyds – unlinked to the overdue Barclay family borrowing – could not be renewed when it matured last year and had to be paid off.

It meant that £35m of the cash generated in 2025 went towards repayments and tipped the business into negative cash flow.

The new accounts show The Telegraph began 2026 with £20m cash in the bank and £15m of its Lloyds loan still due for repayment. With the Axel Springer takeover agreed but not yet completed, the £7m loan appeared to avoid a cash crunch when the outstanding sum was due in May.

data.title: Despite the gloom, Britain can flourish. Here’s how
data.description:
Looking around Britain today, surely only a fool would be an optimist. The nation slithers towards the abyss. Every Budget announces new punishment beatings for business. The state makes a sarcastic mockery of working hard and being honest.

The utilitarian law of globalisation, that price is the only thing that matters, no longer exerts such a vice-like grip over the fate of nations. For decades we have been told that for a fractional base point of additional GDP growth we should surrender strong communities, open the borders and abandon industry.

But the world has changed since the collapse of confidence in globalisation – and in many ways, it’s changed to our advantage. This is a conversation the UK has been postponing. In this context, I shall offer five reasons why Britain can flourish.

Firstly, we have natural energy resources that Continental Europe envies. 

It is obscene to impose the highest industrial energy prices in Europe when we have centuries of exploitable natural gas reserves, plus coal. Although electricity blackouts are probably now baked into the system, we can ensure they don’t keep recurring into the 2030s. 

I have commended the tiny Social Democratic Party’s plan of an emergency “grid stabilisation” of 60GW of new gas and coal, allowing a Messmer-scale building programme of dozens of new gigawatt reactors to proceed. There is no need to race to nuclear, skimping on safety as some of the ersatz “pro-growth” groups insist. Not when reactors last 70 years. An abundance of cheap energy must be our top priority.

Our second important natural resource is minerals. We have copper and gold in Northern Ireland, lithium and tin in Cornwall, and cobalt and rare earths in Scotland. 

There may be even more: as I reported a year ago, we haven’t conducted a national geophysical survey since the early 1960s. Whitehall is waking up to this with some urgency.

Now the third piece of the puzzle can fall into place: by reviving our refining and processing industries. 

British pragmatism thrives in devising new industrial processes. Our petrochemicals sector was once a world-beater, and our excellent chemistry and chemical engineering departments at universities provide the brains. Alas, thanks to high energy prices and policy indifference, this is a sector on its knees.

“If you don’t have a chemicals industry... then you can’t have pharmaceutical production, aerospace production or car production,” Grant Pearson, chairman of Teesside ethanol company Ensus, told The Telegraph recently.

Fourth, British business continues to command respect abroad. 

When I mention this, some readers assume I am being sentimental or ironic. But I hear it affirmed every week. Our reputation for fair play has endured. 

It is astonishing that successive prime ministers and chancellors, from George Osborne to Rachel Reeves, have looked up to the hucksters of Silicon Valley and American venture capital as our model for how to conduct business. Unlike them, we leave something on the table in a deal. Global customers know this, and like it.

Finally, we can capitalise on the engineering and manufacturing talent that creates world-class technology. 

Dyson and Renishaw and Martin-Baker are world beaters in consumer markets, medical instruments and aviation, respectively. “The Germans fear our engineers,” Marcus Gibson, whose research company monitors the health of our SMEs, likes to say.

Writing on the Dyson company blog recently, Sir James Dyson pointed out that nine out of 10 private sector companies are family firms, and employ more than half of all private sector workers. It shows how Labour’s war on family businesses and private property owners is so spiteful. At such times Labour looks much more like a global lobbying firm for hedge funds than a political operation acting in the British national interest.

These five parts are interlocking gears in a modern industrial society; each benefits from the other. For example, a supply of low-cost novel plastics encourages entrepreneurs to innovate and makes prototyping easier.

An industrial revival is not uncharted territory. None of this requires a Stalinist top-down plan or autarky. Government interventions could be limited to giving refining, processing, manufacturing and engineering companies a 10-year amnesty period from tax. 

Other state measures that could help include getting finance to co-operate, which forces successful companies to sell out to grow; and protecting inheritance and strengthening intellectual property enforcement. Other than that, the state should get out of the way and let markets do their thing.

However, this does require something almost unthinkable today: a shift away from the utilitarian logic of globalisation which the UK has embedded. 

This is what I call “performative laissez-faire”. It is performative in the same way that making international climate change pledges is performative: no one else really cares how virtuous we are.

The overarching utilitarian creed is that the consumer must get the cheapest goods, at the lowest price, no matter what the consequences may be for national security or communities. China boomed, while we hollowed ourselves out. 

Surely this ideology is now broken on the rocks. Some will sneer that reviving industry means “picking winners”, but this is nonsense: the phrase should hold no fear for us anymore. Giving industrial sectors a break from punishing taxes would make a refreshing change from the Government consistently picking losers.

The UK has already tried being the management consultancy to the world. Now it’s time to make stuff again.

data.title: Rolls-Royce issues Burnham ultimatum over £3bn jet engine project
data.description:
Rolls-Royce has warned Andy Burnham that his Government must back a £3bn plan for new short-haul jet engines or put 40,000 UK jobs at risk.

Tufan Erginbilgic, the company’s chief executive, said on Tuesday that Labour should pledge financial support to help Rolls-Royce build engines for the next generation of jets being developed by Airbus and Boeing or risk it moving production abroad.

The Rolls-Royce engine programme would create 40,000 jobs, among the best-paid manufacturing roles in Britain, he said.

But while Rolls-Royce wanted to build the new engines in Britain, Mr Erginbilgic said it was also exploring funding agreements with foreign governments that could see the company produce overseas.

“We would like to do it in the UK because of our origin,” he said. “Do we have other options? Yes. We are a business, a global company. I am paid to do the right thing for the company.”

Germany in particular is thought to be keen to secure more work on the engines.

With the two manufacturers expected to select engines for the jets in the next two years, Mr Erginbilgic said the support package needed to be in place soon if Rolls-Royce is to win the contracts. 

Rolls-Royce is understood to have been closing in on a funding deal before Sir Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister. This raised concerns that it may need to make its case again to Mr Burnham.

Mr Erginbilgic said he was encouraged by the appointment of John Healey, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who he suggested was familiar with Rolls-Royce and its agenda, having previously served as defence secretary.

“Obviously there are some different people but the same Government, so in that sense I’m hopeful,” he said at the Farnborough air show.

Mr Erginbilgic said the plan to produce engines for planes set to replace the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 presented the biggest opportunity for British industry in decades.

Missing out on the chance to build the new engines would squander an opportunity that might not present itself again for another 15 years, he warned.

‘Our competitors are fully funded’

Pratt & Whitney (P&W) and an alliance between General Electric and France’s Safran control the engine market for single-aisle airliners.

Mr Erginbilgic said they were benefiting from levels of government support that Rolls-Royce could only dream of.

“Everyone made this like, wow, this is exceptional. It is not. Competitors, some of them, are running the next generation programme fully funded,” he said.

“There are only three companies that can play in this space, and two are incumbents; they get government funding, three or four times as much as I do.”

Mr Erginbilgic said that in seeking to reenter a market that it abandoned 15 years ago, Rolls-Royce also faced a vastly bigger bill than its rivals.

“For us to enter this, we will have to spend much more than they will because I have to develop the product and industrialise it. So I am asking for some contribution.”

The former BP executive, who described Rolls-Royce as a “burning platform” after his arrival as chief executive, said the firm was continuing efforts to secure an industrial partner to help develop the new engine.

P&W, with which it previously worked, is seen as the most likely candidate, though he said discussions were ongoing with “multiple parties”.

“For us to enter into this, we will have to spend a lot more than they will because I have to develop the product and industrialise it. So I am asking for some contribution as governments normally do.”

data.title: Burnham pledges to cap bus fares... but funding descends into farce
data.description:
Andy Burnham’s £2 cap on bus fares has triggered a second major funding row in as many days.

The Prime Minister announced on Wednesday morning that he would cap single bus tickets at £2 from Jan 1 until the end of 2027. Sir Keir Starmer increased the level from £2 to £3 shortly after the 2024 election.

The Government said the estimated £500m cost of the cap would be part-covered by savings on net-zero projects and climate finance. That would include lending money to developing countries for projects to address climate change, rather than handing them the money, as happens currently.

The remaining sum of about £50m would come from Department for Transport funding already set to be spent on buses, it said.

However, Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, failed five times during an interview to say whether interest would be due on these loans to developing countries. She said: “The detail will need to be worked out. We wanted to make the announcement today.”

Mr Burnham’s opponents accused him of announcing another policy without knowing where the cash would come from, a day after one of Sir Keir Starmer’s closest allies said Mr Burnham was unveiling an unfunded plan to cut VAT from electricity bills.

Ms Alexander told Sky News: “The detail of it needs to be worked through. But in order for loans to qualify as overseas development assistance, the terms of the loan need to be reasonably favourable to the developing country and it needs to contribute to developing that country’s economy.

“So it makes sense to switch the spending, instead of being a grant it will be a loan, and that frees up money to spend on domestic priorities and to spend on our public transport.”

Challenged on whether poorer countries may be anxious about whether any interest was due, Ms Alexander responded: “So this is quite standard to have loans for international climate finance. As I say, the detail will need to be worked out.”

Pressed for a third time, Ms Alexander said: “I’m not going to sit in your studio and tell you how something will work when the detail hasn’t been worked out yet.”

Asked again, the Transport Secretary said she was “not going to give you the detail”, and when challenged for a fifth time, she said the question of interest on the climate loans would need to be “worked through”.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast later on Wednesday morning, Ms Alexander insisted she was “100 per cent sure” the bus fare cap was fully funded.

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow chancellor, accused Mr Burnham and his top team of “not actually specifying where the money is going to come from”.

He said: “That is a worrying sign, we need to have a Government which is on top of the public finances, not one that is making lots of spending commitments without explaining where the money is going to come from.”

The Telegraph revealed last month that Mr Burnham wanted to introduce the £2 bus-fare scheme as soon as he took over from Sir Keir.

The announcement marked the second major economic policy to be unveiled by the Prime Minister since he entered No 10 on Monday.

He previously revealed plans to cut VAT on electricity bills worth £850m, which he said would use cash from his predecessor’s abandoned digital ID scheme.

However, the tax cut soon descended into farce when Darren Jones, a close ally of Sir Keir who oversaw the digital ID programme, said the proposal was unfunded.

In a stinging public intervention, Mr Jones told Mr Burnham and John Healey, the new Chancellor, that they would need to find the money for the tax cut at the next Budget.

Capping bus fares at £2 will be badged as an attempt to help people back into work while also helping families with the cost of living. Some city mayors used their powers to keep local fares lower, including in Manchester, where Mr Burnham placed bus services under public control.

Writing for LBC after his policy was announced, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve spoken about the wrong turns Britain has taken over the last 40 years. What we did with our buses is a sorry example. When services were sold off and communities lost a say, fares went up and passenger numbers fell.”

He continued: “The measures we’ve announced this week will help but I know they won’t solve every problem. We need to do more. And we will.

“Later this year, we’ll lay out a 10-year plan to bring down the cost of living, help young people into work and build more council homes. A fairer bus fare is just the start. A fairer Britain is where we all want to be. Let’s bring back hope.”

Andrew Gilligan, Boris Johnson’s former transport adviser, accused Mr Burnham of copying the policy when he was Manchester mayor and Mr Johnson was prime minister in 2022.

In a post on X, he said: “Andy Burnham says the £2 bus fare cap was his idea. It was not. We were working on it from spring 2022, and told Burnham’s team. He decided to pre-empt us by introducing it in September 2022, four months before we did. I’m pretty sure we paid for it, though!”

The new bus fare cap does not cover London, which has a daily cap of £5.25 and a weekly cap of £24.70.

data.title: Rayner blocks 3,500 homes over fears of lead poisoning
data.description:
Angela Rayner has blocked plans for 3,500 new homes in Kent over fears of lead poisoning.

The Northfleet Harbourside project, billed as a major regeneration of brownfield land on the south bank of the Thames, was rejected by the Housing Secretary following a public inquiry.

The proposals, centred on land around Ebbsfleet United’s football ground, included hundreds of homes, a 300-bed hotel, commercial space and an 8,000-seat stadium and had been championed locally as a transformational investment.

But officials warned the scheme risked exposing residents to “adverse levels of lead”, posing “significant health risks – especially for children, pregnant women and the elderly”.

At the heart of the refusal was the site’s proximity to Britannia Refined Metals, one of Europe’s largest lead refineries.

Officials warned the problems with the scheme “significantly and demonstrably” outweighed the benefits, despite the Government’s wider drive to deliver 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029.

People living in flats at the site would be at risk of “chronic exposure to lead”, with levels up to 19 times higher than typically experienced in London.

Officials said: “Put another way, the application site is amongst the worse [sic] places in England to put residential dwellings and public open spaces.”

The scheme also provoked fierce resistance from local businesses and industry groups, including the Port of London Authority, over fears it would wipe out valuable industrial land.

Officials were concerned the development would displace established companies, strip out space relied upon by small and medium-sized businesses and lead to the loss of around 650 jobs.

Particular alarm focused on the effect on Robins Wharf, a facility regarded as crucial to construction supply chains. Ministers said losing it would undermine the delivery of future housing projects.

The viability of the scheme itself also came under scrutiny. Inspectors questioned whether the plans could realistically be delivered, pointing to unresolved issues over land ownership, timing and the overall credibility of the proposals.

The project has been mired in controversy since it was approved locally in 2024 and later “called in” by ministers – an intervention that shifts decision-making power from local authorities to central government.

Further questions have surrounded the identities of the financial backers of Northfleet Central, the project’s developer.

Supporters of the scheme included the local council, some residents and fans of Ebbsfleet United, who stood to gain a new stadium.

The developer has been approached for comment.

data.title: How Labour’s favourite housebuilder became a ‘corporate disaster’
data.description:
When Greg Fitzgerald unveiled plans three years ago to transform his business Vistry into an affordable housing contractor, it was hailed as a masterstroke.

Up until then, Vistry, which also trades as Bovis Homes, Linden Homes and Countryside Homes, had a substantial business constructing houses it funded itself and selling them directly to buyers.

Now Fitzgerald said Vistry would switch fully to a “partnership model”, joining forces with housing associations, councils and the Government to build affordable homes using taxpayer-backed funds.

With Labour on the verge of power, and the UK pushing forward with plans for millions more homes, it seemed the right move from the well-regarded chief executive, who had risen from a building site tea boy to become a FTSE 100 leader.

“So long as the registered providers, local authorities and public rental sector have the funding, there is a great need and demand for new housing from them,” Fitzgerald said at the time.

Investors bought into the story. So did Wall Street and shares flew.

But three years on, Fitzgerald’s gamble looks to have been a major miscalculation.

Vistry shares are down 75pc from £14 to about £3 in the past two years, and Fitzgerald is gone, having resigned in March. And investors think worse is to come.

The company is now Britain’s most heavily bet-against stock, with around 20pc of its shares on loan to investors predicting further falls, according to data from the Financial Conduct Authority.

Some subcontractors have reportedly been told to down tools to shore up cash. The housebuilder has also turned to discounting homes by more than £100,000 to boost sales and produce more cash. It sold just 6,100 homes in the first half of the year.

“It is a corporate disaster of a scale that no one has really wanted to shine a light on,” said one former Vistry insider. “You only need to look at the shares.”

Vistry is one of only two private sector providers deemed a “strategic partner plus” for Labour’s affordable housing scheme, leading it to be called “Labour’s favourite housebuilder”.

But the Government’s hopes of building 1.5 million new homes by the end of the Parliament are significantly behind, and the state-backed building boom has failed to materialise.

Red tape, rising build costs and faltering confidence have all stalled projects across the country and the money Vistry must rely on is drying up.

In a sign of its exposure to government policy, shares rose 6pc on Monday after reports that Labour is exploring plans to reintroduce a “Help to Buy” scheme for new homeowners (Vistry still sells homes to private buyers).

But as much as Labour’s housebuilding problems could be blamed, behind Vistry’s decline also lies a story that former insiders describe not as bad luck, but a failure that was years in the making.

They claim the company’s downfall was built on boardroom capitulation, a strategic overreach and a boss emboldened by his backing from aggressive US investors chasing large financial returns.

The roots of the crisis, according to the former Vistry insider, lie in the 2022 merger between the business and rival Countryside Partnerships, which it is claimed was orchestrated by the British company’s US shareholders.

Both companies had a wide range of vociferous and demanding owners: Boston-based hedge fund Abrams Capital, Browning West, an activist shareholder from LA, Jeff Ubben’s Inclusive Capital Partners as well as David Capital Partners.

The former insider says the Americans were urging Fitzgerald to replicate the partnership model that makes them a lot of money at home – despite what the insider calls a “lack of understanding” of the UK housing market.

“Building multi-storey buildings with a partnerships model isn’t housebuilding. It’s a different animal, it takes different skills,” they said.

Insiders recount how Fitzgerald was courted on two fronts: the US investors “effectively worshipped” him and told him he was “the greatest CEO that had ever lived”, while promising him a reward package considerably greater than what he was on at the time.

“Greg would have believed all of that, rightly or wrongly. He was a wealthy guy anyway; he didn’t need the cash that they purported to be able to deliver to him, but he certainly bought the vision,” claimed the former insider.

Within months of the Vistry-Countryside merger, the company’s US shareholders pushed for a plan for a substantial pay deal for Fitzgerald.

This prompted a bitter row inside the remuneration committee, culminating in the exits of two non-executive directors and a senior independent director.

Vistry proposed lifting Fitzgerald’s total take-home pay in August 2023 from £3.4m to £5.6m a year, which was 28 times the pay of its average worker, according to shareholder proxy adviser Pirc.

The pay package passed despite some shareholder opposition. “I don’t believe the board and the chairman at the time ... fulfilled their fiduciary duty in saying that was not acceptable,” said the former insider. “They just caved to the Americans.”

However, some City sources baulk at the idea that Vistry’s woes were driven by US investors.

“Vistry had made multiple bids for Countryside before any US investors got involved in the process,” said one source, adding that the company’s woes were linked to its old business of selling direct to buyers.

The source said Vistry’s mistake had been not to sell the housebuilding business outright, which is what the US investors had been pushing for. “The business was caught in a situation where it had too many assets and they hadn’t gotten rid of them fast enough.”

Others believe Vistry tried to reinvent itself far too quickly than its operational capabilities allowed.

“It tripped them up,” says a second former adviser. “They dropped the ball on the commercials, and it was a complete own goal.”

A source who used to work for Fitzgerald says: “If there’s a massive structural shortage in social housing that you can address in a capital-light way, you can see that on paper, Vistry’s strategy makes sense.

“But it expanded far too quickly, didn’t integrate the regions and there was no line of control. And then one or two of the regions lost the plot and missed their numbers.”

A string of profit warnings followed, along with a hefty cladding bill, much of which is being spent on fixing legacy Countryside sites.

Fitzgerald, who had added the role of executive chairman to chief executive in 2024, resigned in March, with Adam Daniels – a Countryside Partnerships veteran since 2016 – promoted to chief executive.

Although he has served as chief executive for less than four months, the scale of the job in front of Daniels is already clear.

The findings of a strategic review that he undertook within weeks of stepping into the role will be published alongside September’s half-year results, which are expected to show a £30m loss.

This was announced alongside the exit of Tim Lawlor, its finance chief, last month.

Average daily net debt hit close to £800m in the first half of this year, leaving investors anxiously awaiting a trading update that has been delayed to September.

It comes amid reports that some are pushing for Labour to nationalise Vistry so that it can deliver Andy Burnham’s mission for the “biggest council housebuilding programme since the post-war period”.

Vistry previously denied that any discussions with the Government on the matter had taken place.

Questions remain about the substantial undertaking facing Daniels to turn Vistry’s fortunes around.

The first former insider says: “It’s not a corporate story to cover in glory. The current CEO has got a hell of a job.

“You shake your head in disbelief that a very good business could have allowed pressure from US shareholders and poor performance from the board to put them in this place. I look at it with a huge degree of sadness.”

A Vistry spokesman said: “We continue to have confidence in our business model and the strong relationships we have built with our partners over many years.

“While current market conditions are challenging for all companies in our sector, we are building at scale and pace, delivering the high-quality homes this country so desperately needs, including over 6,000 in the first half alone.

“We have made it clear that we are treating 2026 as a transitional year to improve the execution of our model, while focusing on cash generation and taking decisive steps to reduce debt levels, and we have made significant progress over the past few months.”

Browning West, Abrams Capital and David Capital were contacted for comment. Inclusive Capital wound down its funds in 2023, saying at the time that the public markets had not rewarded its focus on sustainable investment.

data.title: Former Tory donor goes to war over planned warehouse near his mansion
data.description:
A billionaire former Conservative donor has accused an Oxfordshire council of “turning its back” on locals over proposals for a vast complex of warehouses near his country estate.

Wafic Saïd, a Syrian-born businessman, claimed Cherwell district council had “capitulated to developers” after it refused to defend an earlier decision to block four large logistics warehouses near Tusmore Park, Oxfordshire.

Councillors had initially refused Tritax Logistics permission to develop the warehouses at Baynards Green.

However, the local officials have since abandoned their opposition and will not provide evidence when the decision is sent to the Planning Inspectorate in September.

Mr Saïd, 86, is best known for brokering Britain’s largest-ever export agreement in 1985.

The Al-Yamamah arms deal saw tens of billions of pounds of Tornado fighter jets sold to Saudi Arabia in exchange for crude oil, with Mr Saïd acting as a key intermediary between the UK and the Saudi royal family.

Mr Saïd rebuilt Tusmore Manor House, which is close to the proposed development, in 2000, erecting a vast Palladian-style mansion on the grounds. The businessman was also the donor to Oxford University’s Saïd Business School.

The development, which has prompted a fierce backlash from locals, is expected to cover an area larger than 200 football pitches. The data centre plan was labelled “XXL size” by the council’s planning committee.

Mr Saïd, whose wife has given millions of pounds to the Conservative Party, said he had been “dismayed” by the council’s move not to defend its original planning decision.

He said the area around Baynards Green, close to the M40, was “quintessential Oxfordshire countryside” that was “worth protecting”.

The warehouses would neighbour Mr Saïd’s Tusmore Estate, which he has owned since 1987. Mr Saïd said: “I have been custodian of the Tusmore Estate for nearly forty years, and in that time have restored and preserved Tusmore Park to stand the test of time.

“To see that work and the people behind it undermined by short-sighted development is profoundly disappointing.”

Nick Barnes, the chairman of Stoke Lyne parish council, said: “The council refused these warehouses because they were flawed applications. Nothing about those applications has changed. The council’s refusals stand.

“Yet the council has now walked away from its duty to defend its own decisions, with no explanation.”

Mr Barnes added: “Residents have a right to know why, and who took this decision.”

Cherwell district council had previously said the decision to drop its planning defence had “not been taken lightly”.

“The council has had to consider not only the strength of local opposition but also the likelihood of successfully defending the reasons for refusal,” the council said.

Tritax had previously said the warehouse project would create thousands of local jobs.

Mr Saïd and Tusmore Park have been contacted for comment.
