data.title: We must channel spirit of the Victorians to fix water crisis
data.description:
Two hundred years ago, not far from Manchester, a young boy left school to train as an engineer. He would go on to change the city, the country and then the world.

John Frederick Bateman was one of the finest engineers of his era, building the reservoirs that powered the Industrial Revolution and transforming mankind’s capabilities.

This is what the Victorians did. They built.

Our ancestors built the railways that stitched the country together, the docks that connected our isles to the world and the roads, sewers, factories, bridges, hospitals and reservoirs that made our cities. They saw problems to solve, not excuses to surrender.

When laws blocked the solution, politicians changed the laws or made new ones. They understood a fundamental truth that Westminster has now forgotten: you can just do stuff.

The Victorians did not waste decades trapped in battles against the consultants, lawyers and lobbyists who today use Britain’s cumbersome planning system to stop growth. Rather, Parliament passed bespoke private acts for specific projects: Manchester received multiple reservoir acts between 1847 and 1879 whilst Glasgow, Birmingham, Liverpool and London all received their own. When a city needed a reservoir, Parliament passed a law to build it.

In fact, these specialised acts bypassed the blockers by design, exempting projects from laws that would have unnecessarily delayed construction. So many came forward that Parliament eventually standardised the process, rolling the most common clauses into two acts.

Together, the Lands Clauses Consolidation Act 1845 and Waterworks Clauses Act 1847 created a ready-made template for reservoirs. Parliament no longer had to start from scratch: new private acts could incorporate the standard clauses, making only minor changes to suit the circumstances of each scheme. This made it cheaper and faster for businesses to build because it prevented delays and gave them certainty.

Our politicians continued to deploy this practice to fix Britain’s water system into the 20th century.

In 1963, for example, Parliament passed the Clywedog Reservoir Joint Authority Act, cutting through the obstacles to construction and creating one body with one responsibility: building the reservoir. Objections were heard and weighed and MPs chose to approve it. Four years later, the reservoir was finished.

Yet again, our politicians showed that you can just overrule objections and get stuff done.

Today, our politicians do not get things done. Instead, they have created a system that stops us from solving problems. It is a labyrinth of consultations and reviews, reports and regulations, legal challenges and endless, nonsensical objections. Ambitions and solutions that were once supported by Westminster now face decades of delays, with no guarantee of approval at the end.

It is the British people and our industries that suffer most.

Summer after summer, we face water shortages and hosepipe bans. This summer, parts of the country are in a drought and around 20 million people have faced restrictions on their water supplies. Yet while previous generations would have acted to end the emergency, to save our households and our industries, our politicians chose to accept decline.

England has not built a major new reservoir for over 30 years. In that time, demand has grown, our summers appear to be getting drier, our winters wetter and the gap between supply and demand has increased.

This is not a problem that can be solved by efficiency alone: even if we fixed every current leak in the South East, we would still need new capacity equivalent to the daily consumption of more than five million households. Whatever the causes of rising demand, one fact is unavoidable: Britain needs far more water storage than it has today – and fast.

Though Westminster has recognised the need to act – the Government designated proposed reservoirs in East Anglia and Lincolnshire as “nationally significant” last year – it has failed to recognise the scale and urgency of the emergency.

Abingdon Reservoir, for example, was first proposed in the 1990s. Located in Oxfordshire, it would be Britain’s second-largest reservoir and help supply 15 million people with water. Alongside other projects such as East West Rail, the reservoir would support the Oxbridge growth corridor, adding almost £80bn to the UK economy by 2035.

In practice, this means new businesses starting, scaling and succeeding in Britain, not abroad, with manufacturers investing with confidence instead of worrying about water shortages and families enjoying the freedom to water their own garden in the height of summer without another hosepipe ban.

The problem is that Abingdon Reservoir won’t be ready for another 14 years – even if everything goes to plan. Should it receive approval from Britain’s planning system, construction won’t start until 2029 and it won’t be finished until 2040. Around half a century will have passed between identifying the need and meeting it.

Government after government has failed to take the radical action required to bypass the blockers and get reservoirs such as Abingdon built. In January last year, the chancellor announced funding and support for a raft of infrastructure projects, including the reservoir, to kickstart economic growth in the Oxbridge corridor – but little of substance has happened.

Today, it still takes too long and costs too much to build in Britain. It is now time to end the excuses.

Andy Burnham must think like a Victorian. His first step must be a specialised Abingdon Reservoir Act, bypassing the consultants, lawyers, lobbyists and processes that are failing the British people.

Rather than waiting for permission, Parliament should grant it, clear the obstacles and have the reservoir built. The act must appoint a chief executive with direct responsibility for delivery, set out the project’s exact scope and create financial incentives for success – bonuses for delivering early or on time and penalties such as pay deductions for delays and overruns.

This should become the model for building reservoirs across the country.

Abingdon will not solve Britain’s water emergency alone and the Government must pass legislation approving other reservoirs and start building immediately. Just as the Victorians once did, it will be necessary for Parliament to pass standardised legislation that future projects can copy, accelerating construction nationwide.

Today, Westminster faces the same choice that confronted Bateman’s generation: accept decline or build the solutions. The Victorians were successful because they understood that progress requires action, not excuses. To end decline and to save Britain, Burnham must channel this Victorian spirit that built his city and our country, and just do stuff once more.

Dr Lawrence Newport is the chief executive and co-founder of Looking for Growth, the political movement to end decline and save Britain.

Today, our politicians do not get things done. Instead, they have created a system that stops us from solving problems. It is a labyrinth of consultations and reviews, reports and regulations, legal challenges and endless, nonsensical objections. Ambitions and solutions that were once supported by Westminster now face decades of delays, with no guarantee of approval at the end.

It is the British people and our industries that suffer most.

Summer after summer, we face water shortages and hosepipe bans. This summer, parts of the country are in a drought and around 20 million people have faced restrictions on their water supplies. Yet while previous generations would have acted to end the emergency, to save our households and our industries, our politicians chose to accept decline.

England has not built a major new reservoir for over 30 years. In that time, demand has grown, our summers appear to be getting drier, our winters wetter and the gap between supply and demand has increased.

This is not a problem that can be solved by efficiency alone: even if we fixed every current leak in the South East, we would still need new capacity equivalent to the daily consumption of more than five million households. Whatever the causes of rising demand, one fact is unavoidable: Britain needs far more water storage than it has today – and fast.

Though Westminster has recognised the need to act – the Government designated proposed reservoirs in East Anglia and Lincolnshire as “nationally significant” last year – it has failed to recognise the scale and urgency of the emergency.

Abingdon Reservoir, for example, was first proposed in the 1990s. Located in Oxfordshire, it would be Britain’s second-largest reservoir and help supply 15 million people with water. Alongside other projects such as East West Rail, the reservoir would support the Oxbridge growth corridor, adding almost £80bn to the UK economy by 2035.

In practice, this means new businesses starting, scaling and succeeding in Britain, not abroad, with manufacturers investing with confidence instead of worrying about water shortages and families enjoying the freedom to water their own garden in the height of summer without another hosepipe ban.

The problem is that Abingdon Reservoir won’t be ready for another 14 years – even if everything goes to plan. Should it receive approval from Britain’s planning system, construction won’t start until 2029 and it won’t be finished until 2040. Around half a century will have passed between identifying the need and meeting it.

Government after government has failed to take the radical action required to bypass the blockers and get reservoirs such as Abingdon built. In January last year, the chancellor announced funding and support for a raft of infrastructure projects, including the reservoir, to kickstart economic growth in the Oxbridge corridor – but little of substance has happened.

Today, it still takes too long and costs too much to build in Britain. It is now time to end the excuses.

Andy Burnham must think like a Victorian. His first step must be a specialised Abingdon Reservoir Act, bypassing the consultants, lawyers, lobbyists and processes that are failing the British people.

Rather than waiting for permission, Parliament should grant it, clear the obstacles and have the reservoir built. The act must appoint a chief executive with direct responsibility for delivery, set out the project’s exact scope and create financial incentives for success – bonuses for delivering early or on time and penalties such as pay deductions for delays and overruns.

This should become the model for building reservoirs across the country.

Abingdon will not solve Britain’s water emergency alone and the Government must pass legislation approving other reservoirs and start building immediately. Just as the Victorians once did, it will be necessary for Parliament to pass standardised legislation that future projects can copy, accelerating construction nationwide.

Today, Westminster faces the same choice that confronted Bateman’s generation: accept decline or build the solutions. The Victorians were successful because they understood that progress requires action, not excuses. To end decline and to save Britain, Burnham must channel this Victorian spirit that built his city and our country, and just do stuff once more.

Dr Lawrence Newport is the chief executive and co-founder of Looking for Growth, the political movement to end decline and save Britain.

data.title: Ryanair crew failed to help passenger almost sucked out of window
data.description:
Ryanair crew failed to help a passenger when he was nearly sucked through a window after it shattered mid-flight, it has been claimed.

Ljubiša Karović, 61, from Serbia, fainted several times after he was dragged into the hole during a flight from Thessaloniki, Greece, to an airport near Munich on July 9.

His wife, Svetlana Grković, who was seated three rows behind, rushed to help as the window smashed and oxygen masks dropped from the ceiling of the cabin.

Ryanair insisted its cabin crew had done a “phenomenal job” in responding to the incident involving Mr Karović, before telling The Telegraph that it was conducting a formal investigation.

However, Ms Grković said it was fellow passengers – and not cabin crew – that saved her husband.

She told the Guardian: “I rushed over too. None of the cabin crew helped. It was the passengers. One man, I think he was an Albanian, was incredible.

“He did all he could to bring him in and then tried to block the window, first with a bag that was immediately sucked out and then with a suitcase, which worked. We are eternally grateful to him.”

It is thought Mr Karović was “half in and half out of the plane” for up to two minutes.

He said: “They tell me I fainted twice, and again inside the plane, and that my face was briefly swollen and deformed because of the pressure, the rush of air. My wife reminds me about that.”

Vasilis Tsiaras, Mr Karović’s lawyer, said his client “dipped in and out of death”.

The lawyer added: “When the cabin lost pressure he was hurled out of the window from his chest up and immediately lost consciousness. He was on that plane heading to Germany to celebrate his brother’s birthday.

“Instead, at 15,000ft he ended up with his head and right arm outside the aircraft as it moved at a speed of more than 600km/h. He looked at death, that other world, and came back.”

Mr Tsiaras said: “We have no complaint with the pilot, who followed the safety protocols and dealt with the situation very well.

“My client fainted two or three times, once outside the aircraft when he was partially sucked out of the window, and twice inside when, again, he lost consciousness. At no point did the cabin crew offer to help.

“It was the other passengers who rallied and gave Ljubisa water.”

He added that the airline had not even contacted Mr Karović or his wife to offer any assistance. But it had contacted their son, who booked the flights, about rebooking.

In a statement to the Guardian, the airline said: “As soon as the aircraft descended to a safe altitude our cabin crew attended to and assisted Mr Karović, moving him to alternate seats (beside his wife) and arranged for a doctor onboard to sit with them until the aircraft landed safely back in Thessaloniki.

“They also arranged to have medical assistance standing by on landing in Thessaloniki.”

Mr Karović was discharged from hospital this week and is wearing a neck brace.

Doctors have told him he will have to wear it for six weeks, after which they will decide if surgery is needed.

Mr Karović said he should be offered compensation rather than “emails that have focused on rebooking the flight”.

And he urged other passengers to always wear their seatbelt, adding: “I am lucky. My head and neck still hurt, but I am alive. It could have been the seatbelt, the fact that I was still strapped in. But maybe it is fate. I believe in God and I thank him every day.”

data.title: Beijing tax crackdown hits the City
data.description:
Billions have been wiped off FTSE 100 banks and insurers after Beijing launched a tax crackdown on insurance policies sold in Hong Kong.

Prudential, HSBC and Standard Chartered – which all make significant sums in Asia – shed nearly £26bn on Wednesday after reports that Chinese tax authorities had started charging income tax on offshore insurance policies.

Early enforcement cases in Beijing and Hangzhou reportedly show that policies taken out in Hong Kong have been hit with a 20pc tax.

The move is part of a wider crackdown by Beijing on mainland residents putting money into financial products sold in the former British colony.

Currently, the dividend and interest earned on Hong Kong insurance policies are tax-free.

Beijing wants to close the loophole by charging 20pc on the earnings, bringing Hong Kong into line with the mainland.

Philip Kett, an analyst at Jefferies, said: “Clearly, charging 20pc tax on the returns from insurance policies will reduce the value to the consumer.”

Prudential fell as much as 13.2pc, its biggest drop since the early days of Covid lockdown in March 2020. More than £3.6bn was wiped off its valuation.

The company makes most of its insurance revenue, around $2.2bn (£1.6bn), from policies sold in offshore Hong Kong and Macau, with just $621m made in mainland China.

China-exposed banks HSBC and Standard Chartered also sank more than 6pc each, reducing their value by £18.9bn and £3.2bn respectively.

The three companies were the worst performers on the FTSE 100 on Wednesday.

China has launched a crackdown on taxes going back as far as 2000, targeting the ultra-rich in an effort to fill its fiscal black hole.

Chinese banks and other financial institutions have been told to review overseas investments by wealthy Chinese people to check if income has been declared, according to the Financial Times.

However, analysts at Jefferies insisted the crackdown from Beijing could prove helpful in the long run.

Mr Kitt added: “Markets prefer known headwinds to unquantifiable tail risks.

“Though the immediate market reaction is clearly negative, we suspect that when the shares settle, the market could well take a very different view.”

Prudential, HSBC and Standard Chartered were contacted for comment.

data.title: Royal Navy submarine supplier weighs selling off core division
data.description:
A 143-year-old supplier for Britain’s fleet of nuclear submarines is in talks to break up its business.

Goodwin, which is making parts for the new Dreadnought nuclear deterrent, confirmed on Friday it is considering offloading a “substantial part” of its mechanical engineering division.

This includes Goodwin Steel Castings, its plant in Stoke-on-Trent, which designs precise metal components for the propulsion systems of submarines and the launchers used for Trident missiles.

Shares in Goodwin, which is valued at £1.5bn on the FTSE 250, surged by as much as 10.6pc to hit a four-month high on Friday.

The company said: “Discussions are ongoing and there can be no certainty that a transaction will be entered into.”

The company, which remains half-owned by its founding family, is a key supplier to multiple UK and US frigate and submarine programmes.

It manufactures parts for the Royal Navy’s Astute-class attack submarines and the Dreadnought programme, the UK’s £41bn fleet that will carry Trident nuclear missiles. The first vessel is expected to enter service in the early 2030s.

The sensitivities around the defence assets mean any sale could raise national security questions, with any deal and buyers facing scrutiny in Britain and the US.

Shares of Goodwin had been down 11pc so far this year after a series of disappointing results.

The company revealed in March that it had lost out on a contract to supply coastal radar antenna and transceivers in Estonia. It was also forced to request to delay the dispatch of valves to the Middle East in light of the Iran war.

Shares also fell heavily in November last year when it emerged the Goodwin family sold part of their stake.

Several buyout firms have submitted expressions of interest to the London-listed engineer in recent weeks, according to the Financial Times.

More than half of its £287m of forward orders is made up of defence contracts, which also include work to supply components for the Aukus security partnership between Britain, Australia and the US.

Goodwin’s steel castings business, which has operated since 1883, started when the family first rented an old colliery building in Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent.

It also supplies sectors including aerospace, automotive, construction, fire protection, jewellery, mining and oil and gas.

Along with its defence operations, its work has included supplying parts for the Sir David Attenborough polar research vessel.

The ship attracted global attention in 2016 after an online poll to name the vessel was won by the suggestion Boaty McBoatface. Its remotely controlled submersibles were eventually given the title.

A growing list of UK defence companies has quit the London Stock Exchange in recent years. Cobham, Ultra and Meggitt have all been taken over by US rivals or buyout funds.

Bankers at Rothschild & Co are advising Goodwin on the strategic review.

data.title: London taxi drivers risk black cab shortage
data.description:
London taxi drivers face the threat of a black cab shortage after a Chinese manufacturer radically scaled back production.

Drivers and fleet operators in the capital have complained of nine-month waiting times for even small numbers of cars from the London Electric Vehicle Company (LEVC), which is currently the sole manufacturer available.

Dwindling demand for black cabs means the Coventry-based group, owned by Chinese giant Geely, has cut production of the celebrated vehicles as the popularity of ride-hailing apps lead to fewer drivers.

But its “build-to-order” policy has been blamed for creating a shortfall of electric taxis, just as net zero rules imposed by Transport for London (TfL) force drivers to retire their older diesel vehicles and buy new ones.

At the moment, mainstream manufacturers such as Ford, Stellantis and Nissan do not produce a London taxi because it would not be financially viable, leaving LEVC’s electric TX cab as the only option.

Mick Walker, the secretary of the London Cab Drivers Club, said: “Everyone is starting to realise the trade is in serious trouble.

“There are drivers being put out of work now because they cannot actually get a vehicle.”

Steve McNamara, the general secretary of the Licenced Taxi Drivers’ Association, stressed that the secondhand market for black cabs remained healthy, giving individuals an alternative option.

But he warned that things were particularly tough for fleet operators that only buy new.

Colts Cabs, London’s largest fleet operator with more than 1,000 cabs, typically replaces between 100 and 200 vehicles per year but said it had been offered just 10 cars when it attempted to order 30 in March.

Mr McNamara said: “Fleets are really struggling to get hold of new vehicles.

“In recent weeks and months, there have been attempts to place orders for 200 cabs and people are being told they can only have 25 and not until February next year at the earliest.”

An LEVC spokesman said the company “regularly adjusts manufacturing output to meet expected market demand” but insisted that the cuts to production were also the result of work to gear up for the launch of a new model.

He added: “In the meantime, TX assembly continues and new vehicle deliveries, used sales and aftersales operations continue as normal.”

The most recently available accounts published by the company say it produced 1,308 cars in 2024, or about 25 per week. However, the figure is thought to have fallen since then.

China’s Geely acquired the London Taxi Company, now known as LEVC, in 2013.

The automotive giant, which also owns Lotus, Volvo and Polestar, later invested £500m in a cutting-edge factory in Ansty Business Park on the outskirts of Coventry.

Its business plan assumed demand for its world-famous taxis from London and other world cities, with a van variant also developed as a sideline.

However, industry sources say demand in both categories has been disappointing globally.

In particular, LEVC says it has cut production in response to a dramatic decline in the number of licenced taxi drivers in London.

Since 2020, the figure has plunged from about 20,400 to 15,900.

However, cabbies argue that the company’s “build-to-order” policy is failing to keep pace with demand for replacement vehicles, creating a vicious feedback loop where cars become even less affordable and more drivers are squeezed out.

Under TfL rules related to air quality, black cabs must be retired after 12 years.

The policy will mean some 1,300 cars are taken off the streets in the next 11 months alone, according to the London Cab Drivers Club.

At the same time, rising input costs and high interest rates have pushed up the cost of LEVC’s electric taxis.

When the TX was introduced in 2018, the base purchase price stood at under £55,000. It has since increased to more than £74,000 – with cabbies who cannot afford this upfront cost typically paying more than £90,000 when financing deals are taken into account.

LEVC has blamed this rising cost of ownership for falling demand, as well as the shrinking number of drivers taking “The Knowledge” test and entering the trade.

Whereas some 3,400 people applied in 2000, only 809 people did so last year – with only 107 passing.

Mr Walker blamed the drop on the ease with which drivers can now qualify instead as a private hire operator and then ply London for work on apps such as Uber and Bolt.

Whereas it typically takes three to four years to memorise the hundreds of routes they could be tested on, he said, a private hire driver can obtain a licence in just three to four weeks.

“There’s no one coming into the trade, really,” he warned, pointing to figures showing that last week just one black-cab driver qualified compared to more than 600 private hire drivers.

There are some 109,700 private hire drivers in London overall.

data.title: Burnham’s industrial dream is bound to disappoint
data.description:
Whatever his weaknesses, Andy Burnham, Britain’s new Prime Minister, undoubtedly has popular appeal.

We’ll find out soon enough whether it translates into sensible policy.

But one thing in which he unarguably excels is hopeful storytelling, or what rather irritatingly has become known as “vibes”. A case in point is his supposed plans for reindustrialisation.

Nobody will seriously disagree with the ambition. Though factory life can be monotonous and even soul destroying, it can also be relatively well paid and dependable.

People yearn for a half-remembered past of horny-handed sons of toil who actually made things rather than just traded them.

Burnham taps powerfully into this sense of longing for a bygone time with his talk of a ten-year plan to bring manufacturing jobs back to Britain’s once-proud industrial heartlands.

It’s a promise shared by other populist leaders, not least Donald Trump, who may have little else in common with Burnham but has made American reindustrialisation one of his trademark ambitions. 

He’s as comfortable breaking bread with union bosses as he is with crypto-billionaires and plutocrats.

The first thing to know about what Burnham might have in mind is that at this stage, he does not have a plan for re-industrialisation at all – it’s merely an aspiration.

Presumably, he does not intend to follow Trump into outright protectionism. As an open, trade-based economy, Britain would have far more to lose from such a policy than to gain.

The second thing to note is that realistically we are talking about at best only tens of thousands of jobs, not hundreds of thousands, let alone millions.

The Prime Minister most associated with UK de-industrialisation, at least among the Labour faithful, is of course Margaret Thatcher.

Huge swathes of UK manufacturing closed during her first years in power, when many companies – exposed by her policies to the full force of international competition – struggled to stay afloat.

But interestingly, she did have an industrial strategy, and she certainly believed that the UK could be a good place for manufacturing investment.

It was just that she did not believe in supporting no hope lame ducks. Instead, she wanted best-in-class, highly competitive, frontier companies. To this end, she was ultimately relatively successful in reinvigorating the UK automotive sector with Japanese implants.

Back to the present. The idea that Britain is no longer a manufacturing economy of any significance is somewhat misleading. In fact, we produce more manufactured goods today in absolute terms than ever before, more even than at the height of Victorian industrial prowess.

But the terms of trade have shifted markedly against manufacturing in favour of services. As a proportion of the economy, manufacturing output has slumped in the past fifty years to less than a third of its previous level.

Most of us can agree that the process has gone too far. It is hard to point to any other advanced economy with such a small manufacturing base relative to GDP, though some come close.

Recent geo-political events have highlighted the importance for economic security alone of making more of our own stuff, and not relying as heavily as we do on imports.

Most of the decline can be explained by the fall in manufacturing prices relative to those of services. Domestic demand for manufactured goods has moreover remained pretty much static, whereas demand for services has soared.

But it is also true that productivity in manufacturing failed to keep pace with many overseas peers. Lack of international competitiveness in manufacturing is a large part of the story.

Over the decades, numerous attempts by numerous governments have been made to reverse or at least mitigate this decline. None of them have succeeded.

Analysis more than ten years ago by Professors Stephen Broadberry and Tim Leunig of the London School of Economics on the effects of public policy on UK manufacturing was damning in its conclusions. Many of them remain as valid today as back then.

Government intervention in the form of promoting “national champions” and nationalisation was in nearly all cases an unmitigated failure, they concluded. Similarly with government purchasing and regional policy, whose effects had been at best erratic.

In only one case – Rolls Royce – did nationalisation result in an obviously successful outcome. The standout failure was British Leyland, but there were many others in aviation, shipbuilding, machine tools, electrical engineering, computers and textiles.

Virtually all the literature on industrial subsidies finds them to be money down the drain. More general campaigns to “buy British” have also had little or no meaningful effect.

More recently, full expensing – allowing companies to fully offset spending on plant and machinery against tax – has likewise failed to shift the dial, though this might have more to do with Brexit than the policy itself.

Few big manufacturers want to invest in the UK as long as the UK’s relationship with Europe remains so uncertain. Better, they figure, to invest within the single market.

So it’s a little bit of a mystery as to why Burnham thinks he can succeed where so many others have failed. In most cases, subsidising factory jobs with taxpayer pounds has proved a complete waste of money.

Last week’s nationalisation of British Steel might be thought a special case in view of the company’s position as a seemingly indispensable defence contractor.

The mystery is rather how the Government allowed these ageing industrial assets to be sold to Chinese interests in the first place. 

But at more than £500,000 per job, based on National Audit Office estimates, the costs of keeping the plants open through to 2028 are off the scale. It would be cheaper simply to pay employees not to work.

None of this is to argue that the UK should give up on manufacturing. What’s left of the manufacturing base tends to be highly competitive, high value and strikingly successful, Rolls Royce being an obvious case in point.

When Tufan Erginbilgiç, its chief executive, demands hundreds of millions in launch aid to re-enter the market for narrow-bodied aircraft engines, he knows he’s pushing at an open door. In aerospace, launch aid comes with the territory. All countries provide it given the chance. You either play the game or you get out of it.

If the Government sticks to its pledge to nearly double the defence budget by 2035, this too is bound to be an important boost to manufacturing employment.

But as for the taxpayer-funded subsidies and bailouts of yesteryear, forget it. Even if Burnham wanted to, he no longer has the money for 1970s-style largesse.

It nearly bankrupted the country back then, and it would do so again if similarly applied today. 

Careful with those “vibes” Mr Burnham. They may work for now, but you can only really disappoint.

data.title: Billionaire Revolut founder sued over £300m superyacht sale
data.description:
The billionaire founder of Revolut has been hit with a lawsuit from a luxury ship broker accusing him of sidestepping paying commission on the sale of a €350m (£300m) superyacht.

Nik Storonsky is being sued at the High Court for €17.5m by Cecil Wright & Partners, which claims it was entitled to a 5pc fee from the yacht purchase.

The firm, founded by Chris Cecil-Wright, alleges Mr Storonsky’s family office approached it in late 2024 about commissioning a custom-built yacht.

The next year, his advisers asked if there was a yacht the billionaire could buy sooner. Mr Cecil Wright’s lawyers claim the firm recommended a 334ft yacht, then under construction.

The superyacht includes a 25ft glass-bottomed infinity pool, a beach club and an on-board gym with a cryotherapy chamber, according to the luxury magazine Robb Report.

But in January this year, the broker was told that Mr Storonsky, who is worth an estimated $20bn thanks to his stake in Revolut, had completed the purchase directly with the seller, the billionaire Patrick Dovigi.

Lawyers for Mr Cecil-Wright argued in its legal claim that it played an instrumental role in the deal.

Mr Cecil-Wright told the Financial Times, which first reported the claim, that it was the first time he had felt compelled to pursue legal action over a lost commission.

He said: “It’s very rare for brokers to find themselves in this situation and it’s the first time I have done so, but I feel strongly about it, hence am taking action.”

A spokesman for Mr Storonsky’s family office said: “We’re aware of the claim. It’s without merit and will be defended. As it’s now a legal matter we won’t be commenting further.”

The yacht, originally commissioned by Mr Dovigi, a Canadian waste management entrepreneur and former ice hockey player, was initially sold to a Brazilian businessman called Daniel Vorcaro, who owned a lender called Banco Master.

However, Mr Vorcaro was arrested in Brazil in November last year amid an investigation into alleged fraud. He is reported to have denied any wrongdoing.

Mr Dovigi is said to have bought back the yacht following Mr Vorcaro’s arrest, before selling it on to Mr Storonsky.

Founded in 2013, Cecil Wright, which has offices in London, Monaco and Jersey, is credited with brokering a series of major superyacht sales, including a deal for Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s 255ft Hampshire II.

Mr Cecil-Wright also worked on the 324ft superyacht Madame Gu, which was built for Russian billionaire Andrei Skoch and reportedly includes an enclosed helicopter hangar.

data.title: EasyJet set for £5.7bn US takeover as Stelios backs deal
data.description:
EasyJet founder Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou has backed a £5.7bn takeover of the low-cost airline, saying the deal will return the carrier to growth.

The billionaire entrepreneur, who started easyJet in 1995, said on Thursday that he would support an acquisition by US private equity giant Apollo after rival suitor Castlelake pulled out of the race.

Sir Stelios said he intended to remain a long-term investor in easyJet, rolling over his shares into new vehicle set up by Apollo, instead of cashing out his £900m stake.

He said: “I am pleased with Apollo’s strategic intentions for the easyJet business, which aim to create more growth.”

It signals a major endorsement in the airline after a brutal period, which saw its share price slump to lows of less than £4 because of surging fuel prices following the Iran war.

The deal also marks the end of a bidding war between Castlelake and Apollo, the $1tn (£740m) New York investment firm, to take the London-listed airline private.

Sir Stelios, who also owns the “easy” brand attached to hotels and gyms, listed the airline on the London Stock Exchange in 2000.

The former airline boss and his family had continued to own a 15pc stake in the airline, down from 34pc a few years ago.

Sir Stelios said: “The ownership of the easy family of brands has generated a steady income stream for me over the last 26 years that I now use to fund my charitable giving via the Stelios Philanthropic Foundation.”

His comments come after Castlelake, an investment firm from Minneapolis, said on Thursday that it would not be making another offer for the airline, leaving Apollo as the sole bidder.

EasyJet agreed to Apollo’s £7.15-a-share offer, with Kenton Jarvis, the chief executive, saying that Apollo’s “experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for easyJet”.

Castlelake submitted its first offer to buy easyJet in June before agreeing to buy the airline for £5.2bn in July.

But the agreement fell apart when Apollo outbid its rival, striking a deal to buy easyJet for £5.7bn just weeks later.

EasyJet extended a deadline for Castlelake to submit another bid earlier this week, leading to speculation that it might come back with an improved offer for the airline.

The bidding war helped easyJet’s shares to surge to its highest price since the pandemic.

Castlelake initially made four separate offers for easyJet, which were all rejected by the budget airline’s board.

However, the airline subsequently accepted Castlelake’s fifth offer in June, when the private equity firm attempted a hostile takeover.

EasyJet had accused Castlelake of making “opportunistic” bids and of attempting to buy the airline “on the cheap”.

The share price increased sharply after Castlelake made its initial bid in June. However, the stock remains down by over 50pc since its peak over a decade ago.

data.title: The green transition will fail if it takes us to the Chinese begging bowl
data.description:
Want to make something in Britain? You’d better be amazing and innovative, because you’re a jockey carrying extra weight. British factories pay around four times as much for their electricity as their Chinese rivals, and about double our European friends. That alone explains so much of what’s wrong with our economy, and so much of what it would take to put right.

It’s also the missing element from the ever-brilliant Tim Stanley’s column in these pages on Sunday. The question for us as Conservatives isn’t whether the climate is changing, we can see that for ourselves. The question is: what we should do about it?

How do we adapt our economy quickly enough to have the electrical power we need to innovate and adjust to a new world? How do we make sure we have a stake in that future and not just the legacy of our past?

If we get that wrong, Britain will go from the cutting edge of scientific leadership, to economic vassalage. The trouble is, that’s exactly where the policies so many of the so-called environmentalists would take us, costing not just Britain but the world.

Let’s start with the numbers. Britain emits a little under half the carbon we did in 1990. That may sound like a triumph, but the carbon in what we actually consume, imports included, has fallen by only about a fifth. That gap isn’t a saving, it’s a transfer. Worse, while we’ve exported the jobs, we’ve increased the carbon.

A kilowatt-hour on the Chinese grid carries around three times the carbon of one here. A blast furnace emits about two tonnes of carbon for every tonne of steel, nearly five times what the electric-arc furnace now being built at Port Talbot will emit. Again and again we’ve priced British carbon to punish, pushed the work overseas and raised the total emitted.

It’s almost as though we believed that net zero in one country alone, and that a country responsible for less than 1 per cent of global emissions, could fix it alone. It won’t. What’s worse, this is a bet against the future and a punishment of innovation.

Almost every technology in the green transition has British fingerprints on it. The cathode at the heart of every lithium-ion battery in the world was discovered in an Oxford laboratory in 1980, winning its inventor a Nobel Prize. Perovskite laid over silicon, the most efficient solar architecture yet built, came out of an Oxford spin-out, and graphene was isolated in Manchester in 2004.

That last discovery tells a story. A British innovation that has generated interest in China so that more than half the connected patents are there. It’s true that China has dominated the development, but if we’re priced out of the innovation, there’s no carbon-free future.

That’s even true at sea. The 108m blades turning on Dogger Bank are cast in Hull, more than 2,500 of them since 2016, including the first recyclable blades in the world. But every rise in the price of power raises the cost of the next idea, and sends the factory that would have built it somewhere else. Everything that costs our economy makes the future more carbon-fixed.

None of this is an argument against batteries, wind or solar. We know that a perovskite panel repays the carbon spent building it within months and then generates for 25 years. It’s an argument about where panels are made.

These have moved to Germany, others to China, but every factory we shut here reopens somewhere the energy is cheaper and that often means coal. How is that decarbonising anything except our consciences? We’ve worshipped net zero and exported the jobs, raised the costs, and the atmosphere has sent us the bill anyway.

That’s just the science. Now for the politics.

Dependency of this kind doesn’t stay commercial. For years many have complained about dependency on the Gulf for our energy, the costs needed to patrol those seas and guard those ports and Saudi Arabia controls about 10 per cent of global oil. China is in a league of its own making over 80 per cent of the world’s solar modules and battery cells, and refining about 90 per cent of its rare earths.

And we know Beijing is thinking about the power in both senses. Last year, they restricted exports of heavy rare earths and the magnets made from them, then tightened the regime again this year against Japan. Loosening and tightening the tap so that no rival supply chain ever reaches competitive scale is about control not commerce.

That’s where the politics of punishment take us, not to the green fields, but to the begging bowl. Britain needs a better choice. We’re lucky to have it.

We can innovate with cheap nuclear at scale so that each small modular reactor isn’t a novelty but a simple permitted development; that would generate export options and deliver more options for innovators. Pumping gas from beneath our own seabed, rather than shipping it through straits Iran can close, would allow that bridge to the future to be built as affordable power keeps the lights on in universities and startups around the country.

And stripping the levies off industrial electricity and breaking the pricing rule that ties every unit of cheap British wind to the most expensive molecule of imported gas would free manufacturers to compete with coal-powered rivals.

Tapping North Sea gas and building nuclear plants isn’t about freezing in a carbon economy but powering our transition. We can choose to invest in the different choices of nuclear, solar and wind but only with cheap energy can we afford to make that change. That’s what Conservative environmentalism should be about: grounded in national interest, economic reality, and scientific fact.

The real answer to Tim’s challenge is more. More power, more ideas, more manufacturing, so that we finally get to less: less carbon, less dependency, less job loss. That’s why we need to be honest with the science and the politics. Take the weight off the jockey and we can win the race.

data.title: ‘Drastic Dave’ to pour £750m into growing Guinness brand
data.description:
The new boss of Diageo has vowed to invest £750m in Guinness in a bet that sales of the popular Irish stout can rise even higher.

Sir Dave Lewis said the spirits maker would invest hundreds of millions of pounds in Guinness amid surging demand from younger drinkers. It will be funded by heavy cost-cutting elsewhere in the business.

The former Tesco boss, who is nicknamed “Drastic Dave” for his record of stripping out costs, set out plans for a turnaround of the drinks business on Thursday as he called Guinness the group’s biggest growth opportunity.

“We’re going to double the capacity of Guinness during the course of this plan,” he said after unveiling a $3.75bn (£2.8bn) spending programme, including a $1bn investment in the stout.

Guinness has outperformed the wider drinks market even as sales of premium spirits have slowed since the pandemic. Net sales of Guinness climbed 12pc in the year to June, Diageo reported, even as the group’s wider sales fell.

Sales of the stout have soared with young people, while the drink has enjoyed newfound popularity among women.

Sir Dave has also been cutting prices on some of Diageo’s biggest spirits brands after admitting they had become too expensive during and after the pandemic.

A one-litre bottle of Bell’s blended whisky is now selling for around £18.50 at some UK supermarkets, down from roughly £25 a year ago.

He said: “Some of the pricing through Covid and thereafter has got a little bit out of whack.

“What we’ve done in the last few months is take Bell’s back to where we think it ought to be, and we’ve seen a volume response.”

The Guinness investment was revealed as part of a broader turnaround plan that will see Diageo find $1bn (£750m) in savings in an effort to revive the drinks giant without sacrificing profits.

Diageo, which also owns Johnnie Walker whisky, Smirnoff and Tanqueray gin, said the money would allow it to “invest in the turnaround without needing to reduce operating profit”.

Investors welcomed the plans, sending shares up by as much as 10pc.

It also revealed it has already spent $514m on redundancy payments in the 12 months to the end of June, up from $73m in the previous year.

While the company declined to disclose how many jobs would be at risk as part of the turnaround, Sir Dave said the biggest changes would fall on back-office functions rather than sales teams.

He said Diageo had “massive duplication” across its global operations after years of building layers of corporate functions.

He also sought to reassure Guinness workers in Ireland that Dublin would remain at the heart of the business.

“Of all the places that I’m investing money, Dublin, Ireland is by far and away the biggest recipient,” he said.

The company is already expanding production capacity after announcing plans earlier this year for a second Guinness brewery at Little Connell in Co Kildare.

It is the first time the former Tesco chief has set out detailed plans for the FTSE 100 business since taking over in January.

Diageo announced the savings programme alongside annual results that underlined the scale of the challenge facing the new boss.

Operating profit fell 27pc to $3.2bn in the year to June. Net profit dropped almost 23pc to $2bn after weaker demand in the US and China weighed on sales. Revenue slipped 3pc to $19.6bn.

The pain has been felt most sharply in North America, Diageo’s largest and most profitable market, where investors have become increasingly frustrated after several years of slowing sales and repeated setbacks.

data.title: BMW drivers bombarded with Spider-Man adverts
data.description:
BMW drivers are being bombarded with in-car adverts for the new Spider-Man movie.

The promotion, which began last week, effectively turns the car’s main screen into a billboard.

Drivers starting their vehicle will see a Spider-Man icon on the internal “control display” screen. Tapping it launches a full-screen animation promoting Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The campaign will last until Aug 10 and is being shown in more than 70 markets. Only cars built after July 2020, running later versions of BMW’s in-car operating system, will show the advert.

The tie-in is intended to promote the latest instalment in the Marvel franchise, which stars Tom Holland and Zendaya, the husband-and-wife actors.

The Spider-Man animation will not be available to UK owners.

BMW vehicles are also set to appear in the film, including the new BMW iX3 and the BMW 5 Series Sedan.

The German car giant called the in-car animation “a special surprise” for drivers to “celebrate the partnership with Spider-Man”.

Bernd Körber, a senior vice-president at BMW, said the film and the carmaker’s latest vehicles both “stand for a bold new beginning and the confidence to shape what comes next”.

In the film, BMW’s “vehicles are not only visible, but woven into the plot”, the carmaker said, “enabling them to connect with a global fan base”.

However, BMW owners have criticised the adverts, questioning why their cars needed to be permanently connected to the internet at all and labelling the animation “slop”.

The new advertising deal comes despite pledges by the German carmaker that its internal display screen would not feature adverts.

In December 2023, Stephan Durach, a BMW executive, said: “To say I’m selling the screen to play a commercial. I don’t see it. It’s a private space.”

Felipe Munoz, an independent automotive analyst, said the tie-in could help the brand reach younger drivers, but it was unlikely to prove meaningful in BMW’s “existential battle” against Chinese car giants.

“It sends the message that while the latter keeps innovating with the state-of-the-art software and batteries, BMW is playing games with Spider-Man.”

The advertising deal is only the latest instance of European car manufacturers offering digital advertising that capitalises on the large touch-screen monitors commonly featured on electric vehicles.

Some of Europe’s biggest car manufacturers have signed deals with 4screen, a German start-up developing similar technology.

Such in-car promotions typically appear as branded pins on a GPS map. Others can appear as sponsored search adverts when a driver looks for a destination.

In some cases, advertisers can also send sponsored “recommendations”, such as pointing drivers towards nearby charging stations or services.

A spokesman for BMW said: “The Festive App in the BMW operating system is designed to provide customers with optional themed animations and messages linked to a range of global and local occasions. It is not a form of advertising.

“BMW subsidiaries decide on a country-by-country basis whether to activate a particular animation.”

data.title: Aldi and Lidl stores to face more competition
data.description:
Aldi and Lidl will face more competition under plans to strip the German discounters of their power to block rival supermarkets from opening nearby.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had provisionally decided the pair should lose a carve-out from planning rules that allowed them to prevent competitors from building new stores close to their own.

The CMA said on Friday that the German chains were now so big that they should be subject to the same restrictions as rivals, which were introduced 16 years ago.

Under current rules, most UK supermarkets are banned from exclusive land agreements that make it harder for rivals to open nearby, boosting competition for shoppers.

The rules apply to Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda, Morrisons, Waitrose, Marks & Spencer and Co-op.

Their German rivals have avoided the rules. When the regulations were introduced in 2010, Aldi and Lidl were made exempt on the grounds they were far smaller than the UK’s major chains, with market shares of around 3pc and 2.5pc respectively, and offered a limited range of bargain products.

Today, Aldi is the UK’s fourth-largest supermarket by market share, while Lidl recently took the fifth spot from Morrisons. Between them, they account for more than a fifth of the UK grocery market.

The CMA said that the pair had grown so large that they should be subject to the restrictions, while they also operate large-format stores across Britain and Northern Ireland and offer a full range of groceries that are directly competing with the UK’s other major chains.

The proposals follow pressure from rival supermarkets, which argued the rules had created an uneven playing field by allowing Aldi and Lidl to use land agreements that other major grocers were banned from using.

Lord Walker of Broxton, the Iceland executive chairman, accused the regulator of moving too slowly last year, claiming the rules were “rigged” in favour of the discounters.

He alleged Aldi and Lidl had been using restrictive land clauses to prevent competitors opening shops near their own stores.

Juliette Enser, of the CMA, said: “We want everyone to have the best choice of supermarket and range of prices when buying their groceries.

“This is about allowing shoppers to choose where they spend their money and levelling the playing field for all major supermarkets.”

The CMA will now consult on its proposals before making a final decision.

Aldi said the CMA’s decision did not affect its plans to open “hundreds of new stores across the country”. Lidl said the review “will not impact our steadfast momentum and growth”.

data.title: Queen offers £2,500 to rising young journalists
data.description:
Young journalists have been offered the chance to win up to £2,500 and career mentoring under an awards initiative being launched with support from Queen Camilla.

The Queen Camilla Future of Journalism Awards will give 25 winning journalists aged 18 to 30 a cash prize for training, equipment, travel, or accommodation, as well as the offer of mentoring or coaching.

The annual award is being run by the Journalists’ Charity, with support from its patron the Queen, to give young journalists working across print, broadcast, digital, and social media the opportunity to invest in their career development and overcome financial challenges to joining the industry.

As well as the cash prize and mentoring, winners will receive an invitation to join industry leaders at a ceremony to recognise their commitment to journalism and their potential.

Applications are open throughout August, with the winners set to be announced in September.

‘Deeply honoured’

James Brindle, chief executive of the charity, said: “We’re deeply honoured that, as our patron, Her Majesty The Queen is backing the charity’s efforts to support new talent at a time when journalism has never been more important.

“It’s a privilege to launch this ground-breaking new awards scheme which is set to unlock opportunities for many younger journalists nationwide.

“The awards will make a real difference every year, giving the stars of the future the tools they need to take their career to the next level.”

Applicants will need to show their commitment to journalism and how a potential financial award would make a difference to their career.

The Journalists’ Charity was founded by Charles Dickens in 1864 and supports journalists across the UK and Ireland.

Queen Victoria was an early supporter, granting the organisation a Royal Charter in 1890.

data.title: Tunbridge Wells urges Burnham to put South East Water into special administration
data.description:
Andy Burnham has been urged to put South East Water into special administration after residents were left without running water.

Dry Wells Action, a campaign group, has written to the Prime Minister requesting he invoke the water industry’s Special Administration Regime (SAR), a form of nationalisation which is also being lined up for Thames Water.

South East Water, which provides water to 2.3 million customers across Hampshire, Berkshire, Surrey, Sussex and Kent, is under pressure after it warned last week that it was facing a cash crunch.

The company, which has £1.7bn of debt, struck a deal on Friday for £200m of funding to help keep it afloat, but concerns persist about its long-term future.

Jonathan Hawker, the chairman of Dry Wells, has urged Mr Burnham to temporarily bring South East Water under government control after claiming it was failing “operationally, financially and institutionally”.

The water company was recently fined £30m after more than 70,000 homes in Tunbridge Wells and the surrounding area were left without water late last year.

Mr Hawker said ministers should begin contingency planning to protect customers and impose a moratorium on construction projects in areas affected by recurring water shortages.

The group pointed to three major failures occurring in Tunbridge Wells alone within the past eight months, the latest of which left around 7,000 properties in the town and the nearby village of Pembury without water on July 18 and 19.

“None of this is bad luck or down to extraordinary weather conditions as South East Water would have the country believe: none of our neighbouring water companies have failed to deliver during exactly the same weather conditions.

“This is all attributable to systemic operation and strategic failures by South East Water and its leadership,” Mr Hawker said in his letter.

He told The Telegraph that this would test whether Mr Burnham is “a man of action”.

It comes as the new Prime Minister makes promises to take greater public control of Britain’s utilities.

He wants to nationalise Thames Water, with reports suggesting he would use an SAR. Its main lenders are trying to block this by offering the Government a “golden share” in the company.

It will also test how much of Mr Burnham’s attention will be focused on the South, having vowed to devolve power out of Westminster and Whitehall to the regions.

This week he opened No 10 North, a new government base in Manchester where the Prime Minister plans to regularly spend time.

‘Systemic and repeated failings’

It has been a difficult few months for South East Water.

Its debt rating was downgraded to “junk” status by S&P Global on Friday after it was beset by supply chaos.

The rating agency said while the £200m funding boost will help, the utility will still have “limited flexibility” until it can access the cash.

Rival agency Moody’s cut the company to junk in May, putting South East Water in breach of its operating licence.

The company has since paid a £30.5m “redress package” to Ofwat, the industry watchdog, and agreed measures so that it can become compliant with its licencing conditions again.

The Drinking Water Inspectorate concluded an investigation into the failure in April, identifying “systemic and repeated failings across both operational control and emergency management arrangements, resulting in serious consumer impact”.

MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs select committee released a critical report in May assessing the utility’s handling of the supply problems.

After the report was published, Dave Hinton, the chief executive of South East, and Chris Train, its chairman, resigned.

A spokesman for South East Water said: “We apologise unreservedly to all our customers for the unacceptable water outages in recent times. We recognise the serious impact this had on our customers and know that we fell short of what is expected of us.

“We are taking direct action to change the way supply interruptions are managed by updating our emergency procedures, improving customer experience and working with local authorities to bolster our alternative water provision.”

The Prime Minister’s office was contacted for comment.

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: Hollywood billionaire Ellison pledges to make more British TV
data.description:
Hollywood billionaire David Ellison has pledged to make more British TV to head off a Labour challenge to the Paramount-Warner Bros merger.

Mr Ellison, who leads Paramount, has vowed to boost investment in original UK shows on Channel 5 after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, threatened to intervene in the $110bn (£83bn) deal because of its effect on media plurality.

As part of legally binding commitments to win approval, Paramount, which owns Channel 5, said new commissions on the channel would “prioritise UK-originated content, including original drama, factual and entertainment programming”.

It has also promised to ensure Channel 5 News maintains its “editorial independence” and to broadcast at least 600 hours of kids TV per year through its Milkshake! shows.

The move meant the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) as well as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the competition watchdog, were able to approve the merger.

The Hollywood tie-up is poised to combine Paramount, which also owns CBS News as well as Nickelodeon and Comedy Central, with Warner’s slate of properties including CNN, TNT Sports and Cartoon Network.

The deal will also affect 4,000 Warner Bros staff in the UK. The Hollywood giant has made several major movies in its Leavesden studios in Hertfordshire in recent years, including Barbie and Wonka.

The CMA cleared the deal after investigating concerns about the impact of reducing the number of major Hollywood studios from five to four.

A CMA spokesman said it had cleared the blockbuster merger “as it does not raise competition concerns in the UK”.

They added that its investigation found that following the deal, Paramount “will continue to face sufficient competition” across TV and film production as well as streaming services.

Separately, Ms Nandy had written to Paramount and Warner Bros just weeks ago saying she was “minded to intervene” in the merger between the two Hollywood giants.

Ms Nandy’s decision not to intervene in the merger between the two Hollywood film studios means that Ofcom, the regulator, will not conduct a formal public interest investigation into the deal.

The Culture Secretary will also meet the Hollywood giant in the coming weeks to secure pledges about the impact of the mega-merger deal on Britain’s wider creative industry.

A statement from the department said that the set of guarantees from Paramount will “help safeguard the continued availability of a diverse range of broadcasting and on-demand services in the UK”.

It marks a boost for the merger which has become bogged down in recent months by a legal challenge from 12 American states.

The US department of justice has already cleared the deal, although it still faces state opposition and clearance from the American communications regulator.

Mr Ellison, a supporter of Donald Trump and the son of the tech billionaire Larry Ellison, has also received pushback on the deal from staff at CNN and Hollywood stars such as Jane Fonda and Ben Stiller.

Paramount has said it expects the deal to be completed by the end of September. However, there are fears that the legal challenge will hold up the merger.

A month-long delay could become very costly for Paramount. The company previously pledged to start paying Warner Bros’ shareholders an added ticking-fee compensation amounting to about $7m (£5.2m) per day if the deal wasn’t closed by Sept 30.

Paramount said it was “pleased to have agreed on a path forward” with the DCMS. It added that the decision by the CMA “directly refutes the assumptions” made in the legal complaint led by the state of California.

Warner Bros was contacted for comment.

data.title: Italy is running out of Italians. A similar demographic catastrophe awaits Britain
data.description:
In the last couple of years I have been all over Italy. Mostly the south and the islands: Sardinia, Sicily, Puglia, Calabria – the periphery, the Mezzogiorno, the places where every travel writer is contractually obliged to note the picturesque decay alongside the antique dazzle.

And yes, I noted it. The crumbling palazzi, the feral verges, the towns half-shuttered by lunchtime. In the deep south you expect this. It is part of the deal, almost part of the charm. And Italy and Italians can still be wildly charming.

But in the last month I have been somewhere else. First the allegedly affluent north-east, around Trieste. Then, in the past week, I’ve been touring the wealthy industrial heartland south of Milan – the Po Valley, Pavia, Piacenza – the flatlands where Italy actually makes its manufacturing money.

And, I confess, I’ve been shocked. Because the chaos and decay of the south are now spreading right across Il Bel Paese.

The first thing you notice is the roads. Mamma Mia, are they bad. You can be driving on a main road between two proper towns and every hundred metres there is a pothole big enough to swallow a Fiat 500. Or so it feels. After a week of swerving, my nerves are shot and my axles are not much better. And my anxiety is based on hard fact. I checked.

In 2014 Rome half-abolished Italy’s provinces. It scrapped their elected governments, stripped their budgets – but left them owning 130,000 kilometres of road. Maintenance became a fiction. By 2017 provincial presidents were filing formal complaints with public prosecutors: legally covering themselves for the day the busted tarmac murdered someone. A year later, Genoa’s Morandi bridge fell into the Polcevera.

Last year the government announced a 70 per cent cut to provincial road funds, with Emilia-Romagna, the very region I’ve been rattling across, slated to lose half its money. Provincial chiefs warned that the only remaining option would be to close roads altogether.

Once you’ve noticed the dodgy roads, you start seeing everything else. The abandoned factories with their smashed skylights. The tatty, dying shopping centres. The graffiti almost everywhere.

This is what European decline looks like, and it has numbers attached.

Italy is the only major economy where real wages are lower than they were in 1990. GDP per head has barely budged since the euro arrived. Car production – in the land of Fiat, Alfa and Lancia – has collapsed to levels last seen in the 1950s.

Meanwhile, China has swallowed the textiles, shoes and furniture that once meant “Made in Italy” was an honourable boast.

And beneath it all is something starker: Italy is running out of Italians. Last year the country recorded 355,000 births – an all-time low and down nearly 40 per cent since 2008 – against 652,000 deaths. That is a natural loss of almost 300,000 people: a Verona, erased, annually. With a fertility rate of 1.14 and a median age of 49.1, Italy the oldest country in the EU.

What looks like decay may simply be what a very old country looks like – too few young workers to patch the tarmac, too few young families to fill the shops, too few taxpayers to pay for any of it.

We British love to tell ourselves we are uniquely doomed. We are not. In 1987 Italy celebrated “il sorpasso” – the moment its economy overtook ours. Nobody in Rome mentions il sorpasso now.

But before we get remotely superior, note the direction of travel: an ageing society, flatlining productivity, a state that cannot fix the basics. Italy may be the future of every Western nation that can’t make babies, and can’t compete with China.

I ended my latest Italian sojourn in a station bar full of young people in a little moonlit town near Piacenza. It was Sunday night. It was the World Cup final.

Italy, of course, was not playing. The Azzurri are now the first world champions in history to miss three consecutive World Cup tournaments. They have not kicked a ball at a finals since 2014, and this time they could not even qualify for a 48-team tournament.

The bar was, therefore, full of Italian kids who can barely remember their country competing at a World Cup. Yet they turned up anyway. And they dutifully watched other nations contest the final match – with a mixture of beery apathy and confected excitement.

Then at the whistle they said their ciaos and they pecked their kisses – and they silently dispersed, into the sultry darkness, down the winding, potholed roads.

data.title: More than 1,000 new homes a day needed to hit Labour’s housing target
data.description:
More than 1,000 new homes need to be built each day to hit Labour’s housebuilding targets, new research shows.

Housebuilders would need to double their current pace of construction, with just 547 homes being built every day, according to figures from Land Value Calculator (LVC).

Labour has pledged to build 1.5 million homes before the end of the current parliament. But even in the best year on record, 2020, only 679 homes a day were built on average.

The figures suggest that builders need to complete hundreds more homes each day and sustain that rate for the next three years to hit the target.

Researchers at LVC said the Government had fallen behind its required building rate by 200,000 homes.

A spokesman for LVC said: “No independent analyst currently thinks that the Government is on track to hit its target.

“New-build starts have risen 43pc from their mid-2024 trough, which is the strongest argument that delivery accelerates from here.

“But at 130,170 a year, they remain a quarter below 2023 and below the current rate of completions.”

“A change of prime minister does not change the arithmetic. The clock holds whoever is in No 10 to the promise,” they added.

For Andy Burnham to meet Labour’s 2024 election manifesto pledge, the pace of building will need to increase to 367,700 homes a year.

Angela Rayner, who has been reappointed as the Housing Secretary, recently admitted that the 1.5 million-home ambition set “a really difficult stretch target”. However, she said she was “not dropping it”.

She said last weekend the target was “very challenging before, when I came into government”.

“It’s certainly got more challenging, and we’ve seen things like construction costs go up, which has had a real negative impact on that,” she said.

Mr Burnham has also promised to launch the biggest council house-building drive in decades.

However, housebuilders are struggling with weak buyer demand as well as tax increases, surging build costs and political uncertainty.

Britain’s pool of prospective buyers has also shrunk under the weight of changes to Help to Buy and higher stamp duty surcharges.

Persistently high mortgage rates – caused by three successive inflation shocks triggered by the pandemic and the wars in Ukraine and Iran – have also eroded affordability.

Uncertainty has increased after Mr Burnham hinted he would look at reforming council tax for homeowners. However, his officials have insisted that he is not “actively considering” any proposals.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “This data does not take into account that we expect housebuilding to ramp up as more of our reforms start to take effect.

“These reforms include tackling blockages in the planning system, backing builders with a £16bn National Housing Bank and investing £39bn in social and affordable housing – and we have already seen housing starts up 15pc on last year.”

data.title: Burnham casts build-to-rent developers into chaos
data.description:
Construction of rental homes has plunged to a 12-year low amid fears regarding Andy Burnham’s property tax plans.

Just 3,455 build-to-rent projects started between April and June this year, down 80pc on the same period last year, hitting the lowest level since 2014, new figures showed.

Regions outside London bore the brunt of the slowdown, with construction falling 84pc year on year from 13,893 homes to 2,176, according to the figures from Savills and Real Estate:UK.

Analysts believe the fall was fuelled by speculation linked to Mr Burnham’s tax policies.

Kate Butler, from Real Estate:UK, said rumours of significant tax and regulatory changes had been “unhelpful”.

She said: “The speculation around proportional property tax or land value tax has also been unhelpful and has had similar effects to the speculation around rent controls.”

The Government has sought to clarify its policy on rent controls, with Angela Rayner ruling them out and officials signalling wider property tax reform is not imminent.

However, with the Budget not scheduled until Oct 28, there may be no rebound in activity until Mr Burnham spells out his plans.

Build-to-rent has been a pillar of Labour’s drive to deliver 1.5 million homes this Parliament.

This has included restarting an initiative to allocate nearly £2bn of loan guarantees to private rented property developers.

Mr Burnham himself has championed build-to-rent projects across Manchester for several years, providing financial backing to major rental housing skyscrapers across the city.

Marcus Dixon, from JLL, said political uncertainty had reinforced wider commercial pressures already weighing on the market.

He said: “The speculation definitely hasn’t helped. There’s a view among investors that they will just wait until all of these things settle and find out exactly the Government’s position before they commit to projects.”

Mr Dixon also warned that the slowdown risked undermining Labour’s wider housebuilding ambitions.

He said: “All of this means that we’re going to see fewer homes delivered. While it might mean we get more homes over the longer term, it makes the 1.5 million homes target seem further and further away.”

Under build-to-rent, purpose-built flats are managed by an investment group, which collects rents to cover the initial construction costs and later reaps the profit.

Schemes under construction have also thinned out, with the number of homes being built nationally down 21pc year-on-year in the second quarter.

A Housing Department spokesman said: “We know how vital the build-to-rent sector is in providing homes for people across the country, and we’re supporting the sector to grow.”

data.title: I know you’re on the phone, do you know you’re in my carriage?
data.description:
I was already having a difficult morning on Thursday, coming to terms with England’s defeat to Argentina when I arrived at my local station to learn that the line was “part-suspended”.

Several barely audible platform announcements later, I found myself in a crammed carriage sitting opposite one of those people who feels the need to main-character their way through the morning commute.

Seemingly recording a live episode of his day that absolutely no one subscribed to, this boorish individual was shouting so loudly on his mobile that his colleagues in the City of London could probably hear even when he lost connectivity at some point near Baker Street.

As if giving an unsolicited TED Talk to a hostage audience, he proceeded to detail his thoughts about the previous night’s football, his surprise at the carriage being so full “when people should be at home nursing hangovers” and speculating as to whether we would actually make it to our eventual destination with “a woman driver”.

At one point I had to double-check that it wasn’t Dom Joly sitting in front of me in an elaborate disguise.

What on earth is it with these ill-mannered and insensitive Boomers, donating their personal drama to the public domain, without giving a second thought to those around them who have absolutely zero interest in listening to such utter drivel?

I mean, if you’re going to publicly broadcast what should be a private conversation, at least have something remotely juicy to say. Impart some gossip. Slag off the boss. But please don’t spend most of the discussion informing the hapless soul on the end of the line (along with everyone in the carriage) that you are indeed on a train and will soon be in the office.

I appreciate that such anti-social behaviour isn’t the preserve of the middle-aged mustard corduroy brigade. Youngsters these days appear to think nothing of abandoning headphones altogether and treating us all to the sounds of their brain-numbing doomscrolling.

But I cannot, for the life of me, understand why anyone would actively choose to hold a lengthy telephone conversation on a mode of transport that guarantees the call will drop out – not just once, but several times.

When this overbearing idiot wasn’t treating us all to the intimate details of his daily grind, he was shouting: “Can you still hear me” into the receiver.

They can’t but we certainly can, mate.

Moreover, I simply cannot understand the need for people to speak on the phone at all while they are commuting – never mind that loudly. What conversation, beyond a call to 999, can be so urgent that it cannot wait until the office?

Noise-cancelling headphones have now become a necessity to drown out the self-appointed broadcasters who mistake a packed train for their own personal stage.
